6.1

NumPy Advanced

NumPy is the engine under pandas, scikit-learn and PyTorch. Beyond the basics, four ideas make NumPy code fast and short: vectorisation (operate on whole arrays, not loops), broadcasting (combine arrays of different shapes), axis-wise operations, and advanced indexing. Knowing views versus copies avoids subtle bugs.

Vectorisation: Replace Loops

Cell — 1 million order totals with GSTPython
import numpy as np, time
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
price = rng.uniform(50, 5000, 1_000_000)
qty = rng.integers(1, 6, 1_000_000)

t = time.perf_counter()
totals_loop = [p * q * 1.18 for p, q in zip(price, qty)]
loop_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000

t = time.perf_counter()
totals_vec = price * qty * 1.18
vec_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000
print(f"loop {loop_ms:.0f} ms, vectorised {vec_ms:.1f} ms → {loop_ms / vec_ms:.0f}× faster; same result: {np.allclose(totals_loop, totals_vec)}")
loop 228 ms, vectorised 5.9 ms → 39× faster; same result: True

Axis: Which Direction to Collapse

Cell — weekly sales: 4 stores × 7 daysPython
sales = rng.integers(80, 200, size=(4, 7))
print(sales)
print("per store (axis=1, across days):", sales.sum(axis=1))
print("per day (axis=0, across stores):", sales.sum(axis=0))
print("best day per store:", sales.argmax(axis=1))
print("share of each store's week:\n", (sales / sales.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)).round(2)[:2])
[[144 131 163 175 194 117 187] [159 156 172 166 192 123 183] [159 123 159 121 96 184 177] [195 149 133 113 94 94 178]] per store (axis=1, across days): [1111 1151 1019 956] per day (axis=0, across stores): [657 559 627 575 576 518 725] best day per store: [4 4 5 0] share of each store's week: [[0.13 0.12 0.15 0.16 0.17 0.11 0.17] [0.14 0.14 0.15 0.14 0.17 0.11 0.16]]
axis=0 collapses rows (one result per column); axis=1 collapses columns (one result per row). keepdims=True keeps the shape (4, 1) so the result broadcasts straight back.

Broadcasting

When shapes differ, NumPy compares them from the right; a dimension of size 1 stretches to match. No data is copied.

Shapes
Result
(4, 7) and (7,)
──►
(4, 7): the row is applied to every store
(4, 7) and (4, 1)
──►
(4, 7): one value per store, across all days
(5, 1) and (1, 3)
──►
(5, 3): every combination (outer operation)
(4, 7) and (4,)
──►
error: 7 vs 4 don't match
Cell — standardise each column; distances between all pointsPython
X = rng.normal([50, 1000, 3], [10, 300, 1], size=(6, 3))       # 6 customers × (age, income, visits)
Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)                         # (6,3) - (3,) broadcasting
print("column means after scaling:", Z.mean(axis=0).round(6) + 0.0, " sds:", Z.std(axis=0).round(6))

diff = Z[:, None, :] - Z[None, :, :]                             # (6,1,3) - (1,6,3) → (6,6,3)
dist = np.sqrt((diff ** 2).sum(axis=-1))                         # pairwise Euclidean distances
print("distance matrix shape:", dist.shape, " nearest neighbour of customer 0:", dist[0, 1:].argmin() + 1)
column means after scaling: [0. 0. 0.] sds: [1. 1. 1.] distance matrix shape: (6, 6) nearest neighbour of customer 0: 3

That pairwise-distance trick is the core of k-nearest neighbours and k-means (Module 7).

Advanced Indexing and Conditional Logic

CellPython
scores = np.array([72, 45, 88, 91, 38, 64, 79])
print("fancy indexing:", scores[[0, 2, 4]])
print("top 3 positions:", np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:3], "values:", np.sort(scores)[::-1][:3])
print("np.where:", np.where(scores >= 60, "pass", "fail"))
grade = np.select([scores >= 85, scores >= 70, scores >= 50], ["A", "B", "C"], default="F")
print("np.select:", grade)
print("clip to 40..90:", np.clip(scores, 40, 90))
print("histogram counts:", np.histogram(scores, bins=[0, 50, 70, 90, 100])[0])
fancy indexing: [72 88 38] top 3 positions: [3 2 6] values: [91 88 79] np.where: ['pass' 'fail' 'pass' 'pass' 'fail' 'pass' 'pass'] np.select: ['B' 'F' 'A' 'A' 'F' 'C' 'B'] clip to 40..90: [72 45 88 90 40 64 79] histogram counts: [2 1 3 1]

Views vs Copies

CellPython
a = np.arange(10)
view = a[2:5]              # slicing → view (shares memory)
copy = a[[2, 3, 4]]        # fancy indexing → copy
view[0] = 99
print(a[:6], "← changed through the view")
copy[0] = -1
print(a[:6], "← the copy didn't touch a")
print("shares memory:", np.shares_memory(a, view), np.shares_memory(a, copy))
safe = a[2:5].copy()       # take an explicit copy when you'll modify
[ 0 1 99 3 4 5] ← changed through the view [ 0 1 99 3 4 5] ← the copy didn't touch a shares memory: True False

dtypes, Memory and Missing Values

CellPython
big = np.ones(1_000_000)
print("float64:", big.nbytes // 1024, "KB   float32:", big.astype(np.float32).nbytes // 1024, "KB   int8:", big.astype(np.int8).nbytes // 1024, "KB")
readings = np.array([21.5, np.nan, 23.0, 22.4, np.nan])
print("mean:", readings.mean(), "  nanmean:", np.nanmean(readings), "  missing:", np.isnan(readings).sum())
print("reshape:", np.arange(12).reshape(3, -1).shape, "  stack:", np.vstack([np.ones(3), np.zeros(3)]).shape)
float64: 7812 KB float32: 3906 KB int8: 976 KB mean: nan nanmean: 22.3 missing: 2 reshape: (3, 4) stack: (2, 3)

Deep learning uses float32 (or smaller) everywhere: half the memory of float64 and much faster on GPUs.

Advanced NumPy relies on vectorisation — whole-array operations that run in compiled code and are typically orders of magnitude faster than Python loops — and broadcasting, which aligns shapes from the right and stretches size-1 dimensions without copying, enabling column standardisation and pairwise distance matrices. Axis arguments choose which dimension is aggregated, with keepdims preserving shape. Fancy and boolean indexing, np.where, np.select and np.clip express conditional logic. Slices are views that share memory while fancy indexing makes copies, and dtype choice (float32 vs float64) controls memory; NaN-aware functions handle missing values.
6.2

Pandas Advanced

Most analysis questions are some combination of filter → group → aggregate → reshape → join. This lesson covers the pandas tools that do each step cleanly — groupby with named aggregations and transform, merge, pivot_table and melt, window functions, and method chaining — on one small sales dataset.

The Dataset

CellPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 1200
sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": range(1, n + 1),
    "date": pd.to_datetime("2026-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 181, n), unit="D"),
    "store": rng.choice(["Ameerpet", "Banjara Hills", "Kukatpally", "Madhapur"], n),
    "category": rng.choice(["Electronics", "Fashion", "Grocery", "Home"], n, p=[0.2, 0.3, 0.35, 0.15]),
    "qty": rng.integers(1, 5, n),
})
unit_price = sales.category.map({"Electronics": 2500, "Fashion": 900, "Grocery": 180, "Home": 650})
sales["revenue"] = (sales.qty * unit_price * rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2, n)).round()
stores = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["Ameerpet", "Banjara Hills", "Kukatpally", "Madhapur", "Gachibowli"],
                       "region": ["Central", "Central", "North", "West", "West"],
                       "area_sqft": [4200, 6100, 3800, 5000, 4500]})
print(sales.head(3).to_string()); print(sales.shape)

groupby: Named Aggregations

CellPython
summary = (sales.groupby("store")
                .agg(orders=("order_id", "count"),
                     revenue=("revenue", "sum"),
                     avg_order=("revenue", "mean"),
                     big_orders=("revenue", lambda r: (r > 5000).sum()))
                .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False))
print(summary.round(0))

transform: Group Values Back on Every Row

Cell — each order's share of its store's revenue, and rank within storePython
sales["store_total"] = sales.groupby("store").revenue.transform("sum")
sales["share_of_store"] = sales.revenue / sales.store_total
sales["rank_in_store"] = sales.groupby("store").revenue.rank(ascending=False, method="first").astype(int)
print(sales[sales.rank_in_store <= 2][["store", "order_id", "revenue", "share_of_store", "rank_in_store"]]
      .sort_values(["store", "rank_in_store"]).round(4).to_string(index=False))
store order_id revenue share_of_store rank_in_store Ameerpet 28 11907.0 0.0170 1 Ameerpet 248 11260.0 0.0161 2 Banjara Hills 908 11984.0 0.0156 1 Banjara Hills 1131 11965.0 0.0156 2 Kukatpally 16 11860.0 0.0164 1 Kukatpally 270 11810.0 0.0163 2 Madhapur 1181 11960.0 0.0152 1 Madhapur 752 11601.0 0.0147 2

agg

One row per group. Use for summary tables.

transform

Same length as the input. Use for features like "share of group", "difference from group mean", group-wise imputation.

merge: Joining Tables

CellPython
store_rev = sales.groupby("store", as_index=False).revenue.sum()
joined = stores.merge(store_rev, on="store", how="left", validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
joined["rev_per_sqft"] = (joined.revenue / joined.area_sqft).round(1)
print(joined.to_string(index=False))
store region area_sqft revenue _merge rev_per_sqft Ameerpet Central 4200 699845.0 both 166.6 Banjara Hills Central 6100 766290.0 both 125.6 Kukatpally North 3800 723391.0 both 190.4 Madhapur West 5000 788777.0 both 157.8 Gachibowli West 4500 NaN left_only NaN

how="left" keeps Gachibowli (a new store with no sales yet, so NaN); validate raises an error if keys are unexpectedly duplicated — the most common cause of row explosions after a join; indicator=True shows where each row came from.

Reshaping: pivot_table and melt

Cell — long ↔ widePython
sales["month"] = sales.date.dt.to_period("M")
wide = sales.pivot_table(index="month", columns="category", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum", margins=True, margins_name="Total")
print((wide / 1000).round(0).astype(int))                          # ₹ thousand

long = wide.drop(index="Total", columns="Total").reset_index().melt(id_vars="month", var_name="category", value_name="revenue")
print(long.head(4).to_string(index=False), "\n", long.shape)
print(pd.crosstab(sales.store, sales.category, normalize="index").round(2))

Charts libraries (Seaborn, Plotly) and databases prefer long data (one row per observation); people prefer wide tables to read. melt and pivot_table convert between them.

Window Functions

Cell — daily revenue: 7-day rolling mean, cumulative total, change vs last weekPython
daily = sales.groupby("date").revenue.sum().asfreq("D", fill_value=0)
w = pd.DataFrame({"revenue": daily,

Method Chaining and query

Cell — one readable pipelinePython
report = (sales
          .query("category in ['Electronics', 'Home'] and qty >= 2")
          .assign(quarter=lambda d: d.date.dt.quarter,
                  revenue_k=lambda d: d.revenue / 1000)
          .groupby(["quarter", "category"], as_index=False)
          .agg(orders=("order_id", "size"), revenue_k=("revenue_k", "sum"))
          .sort_values(["quarter", "revenue_k"], ascending=[True, False]))
print(report.round(1).to_string(index=False))
quarter category orders revenue_k 1 Electronics 103 796.3 1 Home 75 142.8 2 Electronics 107 810.6 2 Home 54 109.1

Performance and Memory

Cell — categoricals, and avoiding applyPython
import time
big = pd.concat([sales] * 200, ignore_index=True)
print(f"{len(big):,} rows; store column: {big.store.memory_usage(deep=True) / 1e6:.1f} MB as text, "
      f"{big.store.astype('category').memory_usage(deep=True) / 1e6:.2f} MB as category")

t = time.perf_counter(); a = big.apply(lambda r: r.revenue * 1.18 if r.qty > 2 else r.revenue, axis=1); t_apply = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); b = np.where(big.qty > 2, big.revenue * 1.18, big.revenue); t_vec = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"row-wise apply {t_apply:.2f} s vs vectorised {t_vec * 1000:.1f} ms; equal: {np.allclose(a, b)}")
240,000 rows; store column: 14.1 MB as text, 0.24 MB as category row-wise apply 2.52 s vs vectorised 1.7 ms; equal: True
  • Prefer vectorised columns, np.where/np.select and built-in methods over apply(axis=1)
  • Use category for repeated text; read only needed columns (usecols), and Parquet instead of CSV
  • For data larger than memory or heavy joins, use DuckDB or Polars (or Spark) — same ideas, different engines
  • pandas 3 uses copy-on-write: modify with df.loc[mask, "col"] = … or assign, never chained indexing
Advanced pandas follows filter–group–aggregate–reshape–join: groupby with named aggregations builds summaries, while transform returns group statistics aligned to each row for features like shares and ranks. merge joins tables with how=left/inner/outer, validate to catch duplicate keys and indicator to trace matches. pivot_table and crosstab create wide tables and melt returns long data for plotting. Rolling, cumulative, shift and pct_change implement window functions, method chaining with query and assign keeps pipelines readable, and performance comes from vectorisation instead of row-wise apply, category dtypes, Parquet, and engines like DuckDB or Polars for larger data.
6.3

Data Cleaning

Analysts commonly spend most of their time making data usable. Data cleaning fixes types, text, dates, duplicates and invalid values so that every later step — sums, joins, charts, models — gives correct answers. The goal is a cleaning step that is scripted, repeatable and validated, not edits made by hand.

A Messy Customer Export

CellPython
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
raw = pd.DataFrame({
    "Customer ID": ["C001", "C002", "C002", "C003", "C004", "C005", "C006"],
    " Name ": ["  anita rao", "Ravi Kumar", "Ravi Kumar", "MEERA  S", "john d'souza", "Priya", "arjun"],
    "City": ["Hyderabad", "hyd", "hyd", "Bangalore", "Bengaluru", "HYDERABAD ", "Chennai"],
    "Signup": ["2026-01-05", "05/01/2026", "05/01/2026", "2026-02-30", "2026-03-10", "", "2026-04-01"],
    "Spend (₹)": ["12,500", "8,200", "8,200", "₹4,750", "n/a", "15000", "-200"],
    "Phone": ["98480 12345", "+91-9848012346", "+91-9848012346", "9848012347", "984801234", "9848012349", "9848012350"],
})
print(raw.to_string()); print(raw.dtypes.to_string())
Customer ID Name City Signup Spend (₹) Phone 0 C001 anita rao Hyderabad 2026-01-05 12,500 98480 12345 1 C002 Ravi Kumar hyd 05/01/2026 8,200 +91-9848012346 2 C002 Ravi Kumar hyd 05/01/2026 8,200 +91-9848012346 3 C003 MEERA S Bangalore 2026-02-30 ₹4,750 9848012347 4 C004 john d'souza Bengaluru 2026-03-10 n/a 984801234 5 C005 Priya HYDERABAD 15000 9848012349 6 C006 arjun Chennai 2026-04-01 -200 9848012350 Customer ID str Name str City str Signup str Spend (₹) str Phone str

Step by Step

Cell — 1. column names · 2. exact duplicates · 3. textPython
df = raw.copy()
df.columns = (df.columns.str.strip().str.lower()
                .str.replace(r"[^\w]+", "_", regex=True).str.strip("_"))
print("columns:", list(df.columns))
print("exact duplicates removed:", df.duplicated().sum()); df = df.drop_duplicates()

df["name"] = df["name"].str.strip().str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True).str.title()
city_map = {"hyd": "Hyderabad", "hyderabad": "Hyderabad", "bangalore": "Bengaluru", "bengaluru": "Bengaluru", "chennai": "Chennai"}
df["city"] = df["city"].str.strip().str.lower().map(city_map)
print(df[["name", "city"]].to_string())
columns: ['customer_id', 'name', 'city', 'signup', 'spend', 'phone'] exact duplicates removed: 1 name city 0 Anita Rao Hyderabad 1 Ravi Kumar Hyderabad 3 Meera S Bengaluru 4 John D'Souza Bengaluru 5 Priya Hyderabad 6 Arjun Chennai
Cell — 4. numbers stored as text · 5. dates in mixed formats · 6. phone numbersPython
df["spend_rs"] = pd.to_numeric(df["spend"].str.replace(r"[₹,\s]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")

iso = pd.to_datetime(df["signup"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
dmy = pd.to_datetime(df["signup"], format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce")       # Indian day-first format
df["signup_date"] = iso.fillna(dmy)                                          # 2026-02-30 stays NaT (invalid)

digits = df["phone"].str.replace(r"\D", "", regex=True).str[-10:]
df["phone"] = digits.where(digits.str.len() == 10)
print(df[["customer_id", "spend", "spend_rs", "signup", "signup_date", "phone"]].to_string())
customer_id spend spend_rs signup signup_date phone 0 C001 12,500 12500.0 2026-01-05 2026-01-05 9848012345 1 C002 8,200 8200.0 05/01/2026 2026-01-05 9848012346 3 C003 ₹4,750 4750.0 2026-02-30 NaT 9848012347 4 C004 n/a NaN 2026-03-10 2026-03-10 NaN 5 C005 15000 15000.0 NaT 9848012349 6 C006 -200 -200.0 2026-04-01 2026-04-01 9848012350
Never let pandas guess date formats on mixed data: "05/01/2026" is 5 January in India and 1 May in the US. Parse each known format explicitly.

Validate: Rules the Clean Data Must Satisfy

CellPython
rules = {
    "customer_id unique": df.customer_id.is_unique,
    "customer_id format C###": df.customer_id.str.fullmatch(r"C\d{3}").all(),
    "city known": df.city.notna().all(),
    "spend non-negative": (df.spend_rs.dropna() >= 0).all(),
    "signup date valid": df.signup_date.notna().all(),
    "phone valid": df.phone.notna().all(),
}
for rule, ok in rules.items():
    print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {rule}")
issues = df[(df.spend_rs < 0) | df.signup_date.isna() | df.phone.isna() | df.spend_rs.isna()]
print("\nrows needing review:\n", issues[["customer_id", "spend_rs", "signup_date", "phone"]].to_string(index=False))
PASS customer_id unique PASS customer_id format C### PASS city known FAIL spend non-negative FAIL signup date valid FAIL phone valid rows needing review: customer_id spend_rs signup_date phone C003 4750.0 NaT 9848012347 C004 NaN 2026-03-10 NaN C005 15000.0 NaT 9848012349 C006 -200.0 2026-04-01 9848012350

Cleaning doesn't mean every problem gets "fixed": invalid values become explicit missing values and go to a review list, rather than being silently guessed.

Package It as a Function

Cell — the same cleaning, repeatable for next month's filePython
def clean_customers(raw: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = raw.copy()
    df.columns = df.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(r"[^\w]+", "_", regex=True).str.strip("_")
    return (df.drop_duplicates()
              .assign(name=lambda d: d["name"].str.strip().str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True).str.title(),
                      city=lambda d: d["city"].str.strip().str.lower().map(city_map),
                      spend_rs=lambda d: pd.to_numeric(d["spend"].str.replace(r"[₹,\s]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce"),
                      signup_date=lambda d: pd.to_datetime(d["signup"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
                                              .fillna(pd.to_datetime(d["signup"], format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce")))
              .drop(columns=["spend", "signup"]))

out = clean_customers(raw)
print(out.dtypes.to_string()); print(len(out), "rows")
customer_id str name str city str phone str spend_rs float64 signup_date datetime64[us] 6 rows

Cleaning Checklist

Problempandas tools
Messy column names.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace()
Duplicates (exact / by key)drop_duplicates(subset=[…], keep="last")
Text: spaces, case, variants.str.strip/.title/.replace, a mapping dict
Numbers stored as textpd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")
Datespd.to_datetime(..., format=..., errors="coerce")
Invalid valuesRules → .where()/mask() to NaN + review list
Types and memoryastype("category"), nullable Int64
Proof it workedValidation rules / tests (pandera, Great Expectations in production)
Data cleaning standardises column names, removes exact and key-based duplicates, normalises text with string methods and mapping dictionaries, converts numbers stored as text with to_numeric(errors="coerce"), parses dates with explicit formats to avoid day/month ambiguity, and turns invalid values into explicit missing values for review rather than guessing. The steps should be scripted as a reusable function and validated against rules such as uniqueness, formats and ranges, using tools like pandera or Great Expectations in production pipelines.
6.4

Missing Values

Missing data is normal: customers skip optional fields, sensors drop out, systems fail to join. What matters is why values are missing, because that decides whether dropping or filling them will bias your results. This lesson covers finding missing data, the three missingness mechanisms, and the main strategies from deletion to model-based imputation.

Find It (Including Disguised Missing Values)

CellPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
n = 1000
df = pd.DataFrame({"age": rng.integers(18, 70, n).astype(float),
                   "income_k": rng.lognormal(np.log(50), 0.4, n).round(1),
                   "city": rng.choice(["Hyderabad", "Bengaluru", "Chennai"], n),
                   "tenure_m": rng.integers(1, 60, n).astype(float)})
df["spend"] = (5 * df.income_k + 3 * df.tenure_m + rng.normal(0, 40, n)).round()

df.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.08, "age"] = np.nan                                   # MCAR: random
df.loc[(df.age < 30) & (rng.random(n) < 0.5), "income_k"] = np.nan              # MAR: depends on age (observed)
df.loc[(df.spend > df.spend.quantile(0.85)) & (rng.random(n) < 0.6), "spend"] = -1   # high spenders' value logged as -1
df.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.03, "city"] = "unknown"

df = df.replace({"spend": {-1: np.nan}, "city": {"unknown": np.nan}})         # disguised → real NaN
print(df.isna().sum().to_string()); print(f"\nrows with any missing: {df.isna().any(axis=1).mean():.0%}")
age 92 income_k 116 city 20 tenure_m 0 spend 87 rows with any missing: 30%

Why Is It Missing? Three Mechanisms

MechanismMeaningExampleSafe to drop?
MCAR — missing completely at randomUnrelated to anythingA random sensor glitchYes (only loses data)
MAR — missing at randomDepends on other observed columnsYoung customers skip incomeNo — but fixable using those columns
MNAR — missing not at randomDepends on the missing value itselfHigh spenders' totals not recordedNo — and imputation can't fully fix it
Cell — compare rows with and without a valuePython
print("mean age when income is missing vs present:",
      df.groupby(df.income_k.isna()).age.mean().round(1).to_dict())
print("mean income when spend is missing vs present:",
      df.groupby(df.spend.isna()).income_k.mean().round(1).to_dict())
mean age when income is missing vs present: {False: 47.7, True: 22.7} mean income when spend is missing vs present: {False: 50.8, True: 90.6}

Customers with missing income are clearly younger (MAR), and those with missing spend have much higher incomes — a hint that the missing spends are the big ones (MNAR). Dropping those rows would make average spend look lower than it is.

Strategies Compared

Cell — impute income, then check against the hidden truthPython
truth = pd.Series(rng.lognormal(np.log(50), 0.4, n).round(1))      # a fresh "complete" column for evaluation
test = df[["age", "tenure_m", "city"]].copy()
test["income_k"] = truth
test["age"] = test.age.fillna(test.age.median())
mask = (test.age < 35) & (rng.random(n) < 0.5)                       # hide some incomes (MAR on age)
test["income_k"] = test.income_k + 0.8 * (test.age - 45)                # make income depend on age
true_vals = test.loc[mask, "income_k"].copy()
test.loc[mask, "income_k"] = np.nan

from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer, KNNImputer
from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer  # noqa: F401
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer
num = test[["age", "tenure_m", "income_k"]]
results = {
    "drop (= mean of the rest)": np.full(mask.sum(), test.income_k.mean()),
    "mean": SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit_transform(num)[mask.to_numpy(), 2],
    "median": SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(num)[mask.to_numpy(), 2],
    "KNN (k=10)": KNNImputer(n_neighbors=10).fit_transform(num)[mask.to_numpy(), 2],
    "iterative (regression)": IterativeImputer(random_state=0).fit_transform(num)[mask.to_numpy(), 2],
}
for name, est in results.items():
    print(f"{name:<26} mean error {np.mean(est - true_vals):+6.1f}   MAE {np.mean(np.abs(est - true_vals)):5.1f}")
drop (= mean of the rest) mean error +16.8 MAE 25.3 mean mean error +16.8 MAE 25.3 median mean error +13.1 MAE 23.3 KNN (k=10) mean error +0.6 MAE 19.2 iterative (regression) mean error -0.5 MAE 18.7

When missingness depends on age, filling with the overall mean or median is biased; methods that use age (KNN, iterative/regression imputation) recover the hidden values far better.

Group-wise Fill, Time Series, and Missing Indicators

CellPython
df["income_filled"] = df.income_k.fillna(df.groupby("city").income_k.transform("median"))
df["income_was_missing"] = df.income_k.isna().astype(int)        # let the model learn from missingness
df["city"] = df.city.fillna("Unknown")                            # categories: an explicit level
cols = ["age", "income_k", "income_filled", "income_was_missing", "city"]
print(pd.concat([df[cols].head(2), df[df.income_k.isna()][cols].head(3)]).to_string())

temps = pd.Series([31.0, np.nan, np.nan, 33.5, 34.0, np.nan, 32.0],
                  index=pd.date_range("2026-05-01", periods=7, freq="h"))
print(pd.DataFrame({"raw": temps, "ffill": temps.ffill(), "interpolate": temps.interpolate(method="time")}))
age income_k income_filled income_was_missing city 0 55.0 44.1 44.1 0 Chennai 1 NaN 53.7 53.7 0 Hyderabad 18 29.0 NaN 52.9 1 Bengaluru 22 21.0 NaN 48.8 1 Hyderabad 68 22.0 NaN 52.9 1 Bengaluru raw ffill interpolate 2026-05-01 00:00:00 31.0 31.0 31.000000 2026-05-01 01:00:00 NaN 31.0 31.833333 2026-05-01 02:00:00 NaN 31.0 32.666667 2026-05-01 03:00:00 33.5 33.5 33.500000 2026-05-01 04:00:00 34.0 34.0 34.000000 2026-05-01 05:00:00 NaN 34.0 33.000000 2026-05-01 06:00:00 32.0 32.0 32.000000

Decision Guide

SituationApproach
Few rows missing (< ~5%), MCARDrop rows
Column mostly empty (> ~60%) and not importantDrop the column (or keep only a "has value" flag)
Numeric, skewedMedian (overall or by group) + missing indicator
Depends on other columns (MAR)KNN or iterative imputation
Categorical"Unknown" level, or the mode
Time seriesForward-fill or time interpolation
Likely MNARFlag it, collect better data, report the limitation
In ML, fit imputers on the training set only (inside a scikit-learn Pipeline) — computing the median on all data leaks test-set information into training.
Missing values should first be found, including disguised sentinels like −1 or "unknown", and their mechanism considered: MCAR is unrelated to anything and safe to drop, MAR depends on observed columns and can be corrected by imputation using them, and MNAR depends on the missing value itself and biases results whatever is done. Options include dropping rows or columns, mean or median (overall or group-wise via transform) with missing-indicator features, "Unknown" categories, forward fill or interpolation for time series, and KNN or iterative model-based imputation; imputers must be fit on training data only to avoid leakage.
6.5

Outlier Detection

An outlier is a value far from the rest. It might be an error (a price typed as ₹45,000 instead of ₹450), a rare but real event (a bulk corporate order), or exactly what you're looking for (fraud). Detection is statistical; deciding what to do is a business judgement. This lesson covers single-column rules, robust methods, multivariate detection, and treatment options.

Single-Column Methods

\[ z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s} \qquad\quad \text{modified } z = \frac{0.6745\,(x - \text{median})}{\text{MAD}}, \quad \text{MAD} = \text{median}\,|x - \text{median}| \]flag |z| > 3, modified |z| > 3.5, or values outside Q1 − 1.5·IQR … Q3 + 1.5·IQR
Cell — order values with a few problemsPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
orders = pd.Series(np.r_[rng.normal(800, 150, 300).round(), [45_000, 38_500, 9, 2_400, 2_600]], name="value")

z = (orders - orders.mean()) / orders.std()
q1, q3 = orders.quantile([0.25, 0.75]); iqr = q3 - q1
mad = (orders - orders.median()).abs().median()
mz = 0.6745 * (orders - orders.median()) / mad

flags = pd.DataFrame({"value": orders, "z>3": z.abs() > 3,
                      "IQR": (orders < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (orders > q3 + 1.5 * iqr),
                      "modified z>3.5": mz.abs() > 3.5})
print(flags[flags.iloc[:, 1:].any(axis=1)].to_string())
print("\nflagged counts:", flags.iloc[:, 1:].sum().to_dict())
print(f"mean {orders.mean():.0f} / sd {orders.std():.0f} are inflated by the two huge values; median {orders.median():.0f}, MAD {mad:.0f} are not")
value z>3 IQR modified z>3.5 185 1204.0 False True False 220 1216.0 False True False 300 45000.0 True True True 301 38500.0 True True True 302 9.0 False True True 303 2400.0 False True True 304 2600.0 False True True flagged counts: {'z>3': 2, 'IQR': 7, 'modified z>3.5': 5} mean 1071 / sd 3327 are inflated by the two huge values; median 791, MAD 104 are not

The classic z-score misses the ₹2,400–2,600 orders and the ₹9 typo: the two huge values inflate the standard deviation and "mask" the others. Robust methods (IQR, modified z) built on the median aren't fooled.

Multivariate Outliers

Some points look normal on each column but odd in combination — a 21-year-old with 30 years' tenure, or a tiny order with a huge discount.

Cell — Isolation Forest and Local Outlier FactorPython
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor

items = rng.integers(1, 12, 400)
X = pd.DataFrame({"items": items, "basket_value": items * 350 + rng.normal(0, 250, 400)})
odd = pd.DataFrame({"items": [1, 2, 10, 11], "basket_value": [3600, 4200, 400, 700]})   # normal ranges, odd combos
X = pd.concat([X, odd], ignore_index=True)

X["iso"] = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=0).fit_predict(X[["items", "basket_value"]]) == -1
X["lof"] = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=0.01).fit_predict(X[["items", "basket_value"]]) == -1
print("the 4 planted points caught by IsolationForest:", X.iso.iloc[-4:].sum(), " LOF:", X.lof.iloc[-4:].sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3))
ax.scatter(X["items"], X.basket_value, s=8, color="#4ea8de", label="normal")
flag = X.iso | X.lof
ax.scatter(X.loc[flag, "items"], X.loc[flag, "basket_value"], s=50, facecolors="none", edgecolors="#ff7c7c", label="flagged")
ax.set_xlabel("items in basket"); ax.set_ylabel("basket value ₹"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
the 4 planted points caught by IsolationForest: 4 LOF: 0

Isolation Forest isolates all four planted combinations; LOF, which compares each point with the density of its neighbours, misses them here because they sit near sparse edges of the cloud. Detectors disagree — compare a couple and inspect what they flag.

What to Do With Them

Cell — treatment options comparedPython
lo, hi = orders.quantile([0.01, 0.99])
options = {"keep": orders,
           "remove (IQR rule)": orders[~flags["IQR"]],
           "cap at 1st/99th pct (winsorise)": orders.clip(lo, hi),
           "log transform": np.log1p(orders)}
for name, s in options.items():
    print(f"{name:<32} n={len(s):<4} mean {s.mean():9.2f}   median {s.median():8.2f}")
keep n=305 mean 1071.11 median 791.00 remove (IQR rule) n=298 mean 791.14 median 788.50 cap at 1st/99th pct (winsorise) n=305 mean 813.28 median 791.00 log transform n=305 mean 6.68 median 6.67
CauseAction
Data error (typo, unit mix-up, test record)Fix from the source, or set to missing
Real but extreme (bulk orders)Keep; use robust statistics (median), cap (winsorise) or log-transform for models
The thing you care about (fraud, failures)Keep and study; build anomaly detection
Different population (corporate vs retail)Separate segment / separate analysis
Never delete outliers just to make results look tidier — document every removal and the reason. As with imputation, compute thresholds on training data only.
Outliers are detected per column with z-scores, the 1.5×IQR rule or the median/MAD-based modified z-score; z-scores suffer from masking because extremes inflate the mean and standard deviation, so robust methods are preferred. Multivariate outliers that are unusual only in combination are found with Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor or Mahalanobis distance. Treatment depends on cause: correct errors, keep real extremes using robust statistics, winsorising or log transforms, study outliers that are the target (fraud), or split distinct populations — always documenting decisions and fitting thresholds on training data.
6.6

Data Transformation

Transformation changes the form of data without changing what it says: rescaling numbers so features are comparable, reshaping skewed distributions, turning continuous values into bands, and turning text categories into numbers that algorithms accept. Most ML algorithms need at least one of these.

Scaling

\[ \text{standardise: } \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \qquad \text{min-max: } \frac{x - x_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}} \qquad \text{robust: } \frac{x - \text{median}}{\text{IQR}} \]
CellPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler
df = pd.DataFrame({"age": [22, 35, 41, 29, 58, 33], "income_k": [25, 60, 75, 40, 300, 52]})   # one very high income
for name, scaler in [("standard", StandardScaler()), ("min-max", MinMaxScaler()), ("robust", RobustScaler())]:
    out = pd.DataFrame(scaler.fit_transform(df), columns=df.columns).round(2)
    print(f"{name:<9} income_k →", out.income_k.tolist())
standard income_k → [-0.71, -0.34, -0.18, -0.55, 2.21, -0.42] min-max income_k → [0.0, 0.13, 0.18, 0.05, 1.0, 0.1] robust income_k → [-1.1, 0.14, 0.67, -0.57, 8.64, -0.14]
ScalerResultUse for
StandardScalerMean 0, sd 1Linear/logistic regression, SVM, PCA, neural networks
MinMaxScalerRange 0–1Bounded inputs (images), when an outlier won't squash everything
RobustScalerMedian 0, IQR 1Data with outliers
None needed—Tree models (decision trees, random forest, gradient boosting)

With min-max, the ₹300k income squeezes everyone else into 0–0.18; the robust scaler keeps normal values spread out.

Fixing Skew

Cell — log, square root, Box-Cox and Yeo-JohnsonPython
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
x = rng.lognormal(7, 0.9, 3000)                                  # e.g. annual spend
versions = {"raw": x, "log1p": np.log1p(x), "sqrt": np.sqrt(x),
            "Yeo-Johnson": PowerTransformer(method="yeo-johnson").fit_transform(x.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 2.4))
for ax, (name, v) in zip(axes, versions.items()):
    ax.hist(v, bins=50, color="#4ea8de"); ax.set_title(f"{name}  skew {stats.skew(v):.2f}", fontsize=9); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()

Use log1p (log of 1 + x) so zeros are allowed. Box-Cox needs strictly positive data; Yeo-Johnson also handles zeros and negatives.

Binning (Discretisation)

Cell — fixed edges vs equal-frequency binsPython
ages = pd.Series(rng.integers(18, 75, 2000))
fixed = pd.cut(ages, bins=[17, 24, 34, 44, 59, 120], labels=["18–24", "25–34", "35–44", "45–59", "60+"])
quart = pd.qcut(ages, q=4, labels=["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"])
print(fixed.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())
print(quart.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())
{'18–24': 245, '25–34': 347, '35–44': 365, '45–59': 547, '60+': 496} {'Q1': 518, 'Q2': 506, 'Q3': 480, 'Q4': 496}

pd.cut uses meaningful business edges (age bands, price tiers); pd.qcut makes equal-sized groups (quartiles, deciles for customer value).

Encoding Categories

CellPython
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder
cust = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Hyderabad", "Pune", "Chennai", "Hyderabad"],
                     "size": ["M", "S", "L", "XL"]})
print(pd.get_dummies(cust.city, prefix="city", dtype=int))

ord_enc = OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["S", "M", "L", "XL"]])                 # order matters
print("ordinal size:", ord_enc.fit_transform(cust[["size"]]).ravel())

ohe = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False).fit(cust[["city"]])
print("unseen city 'Kochi' →", ohe.transform(pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Kochi"]})), "(all zeros, no crash)")
city_Chennai city_Hyderabad city_Pune 0 0 1 0 1 0 0 1 2 1 0 0 3 0 1 0 ordinal size: [1. 0. 2. 3.] unseen city 'Kochi' → [[0. 0. 0.]] (all zeros, no crash)
EncodingWhen
One-hotNominal categories with few levels (city, payment method)
OrdinalOrdered categories (size, education level, rating band)
Target / frequency encodingMany levels (thousands of product IDs) — target encoding must be cross-validated to avoid leakage
EmbeddingsVery many levels in deep learning (Module 8)

Fit on Train, Apply Everywhere

Cell — a ColumnTransformer keeps all of this in one reusable objectPython
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
data = pd.DataFrame({"age": [25, 40, np.nan, 31], "spend": [1200, 54000, 800, 2300], "city": ["Hyderabad", "Pune", "Pune", "Chennai"]})
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("age", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), ["age"]),
    ("spend", make_pipeline(PowerTransformer()), ["spend"]),
    ("city", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["city"]),
])
print(pd.DataFrame(prep.fit_transform(data), columns=prep.get_feature_names_out()).round(2).to_string())
age__age spend__spend city__city_Chennai city__city_Hyderabad city__city_Pune 0 -1.26 -0.55 0.0 1.0 0.0 1 1.54 1.54 0.0 0.0 1.0 2 -0.14 -1.14 0.0 0.0 1.0 3 -0.14 0.16 1.0 0.0 0.0
Data transformation rescales features with standardisation, min-max or robust scaling (needed for distance- and gradient-based models but not trees), reduces skew with log1p, square root, Box-Cox (positive data) or Yeo-Johnson, discretises with pd.cut for business bands or pd.qcut for equal-frequency bins, and encodes categories with one-hot (handle_unknown="ignore"), ordinal, frequency or cross-validated target encoding. All transformations should be fit on training data and applied consistently through a ColumnTransformer and Pipeline.
6.7

Feature Engineering

Feature engineering creates new input columns that make patterns easier for a model (or an analyst) to see. A model can't easily infer "days since last order" from a raw timestamp, or "is the weekend" from a date. Good features often matter more than the choice of algorithm — but every feature must be available at prediction time, or it's leakage.

Example: Predicting Customer Churn

Cell — raw order historyPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n_cust = 300
rate = rng.gamma(2, 0.04, n_cust)                         # each customer's orders per day
stop_day = rng.uniform(40, 420, n_cust)                   # the day each customer quietly stops buying
rows = []
for cid in range(n_cust):
    active = min(stop_day[cid], 210)
    for day in rng.uniform(0, active, rng.poisson(rate[cid] * active)):
        rows.append((cid + 1, pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01") + pd.Timedelta(minutes=int(day * 1440))))
orders = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["customer_id", "order_time"]).sort_values("order_time", ignore_index=True)
k = len(orders)
orders["amount"] = rng.lognormal(6.3, 0.6, k).round()
orders["discount"] = rng.choice([0, 0, 0, 50, 100, 200], k)
orders["category"] = rng.choice(["Grocery", "Fashion", "Electronics"], k, p=[0.6, 0.3, 0.1])
cutoff = pd.Timestamp("2026-06-01")              # features use only data before this date
history = orders[orders.order_time < cutoff]
print(history.head(3).to_string()); print(len(history), "orders before cutoff")
customer_id order_time amount discount category 0 24 2026-01-01 03:18:00 275.0 0 Electronics 1 147 2026-01-01 05:28:00 549.0 0 Fashion 2 140 2026-01-01 06:50:00 413.0 0 Fashion 2575 orders before cutoff

Date and Time Features

CellPython
t = history.order_time
time_feats = pd.DataFrame({"hour": t.dt.hour, "weekday": t.dt.day_name().str[:3],
                           "is_weekend": t.dt.dayofweek >= 5, "month": t.dt.month,
                           "hour_sin": np.sin(2 * np.pi * t.dt.hour / 24).round(3),
                           "hour_cos": np.cos(2 * np.pi * t.dt.hour / 24).round(3)})
print(time_feats.head(4).to_string())
hour weekday is_weekend month hour_sin hour_cos 0 3 Thu False 1 0.707 0.707 1 5 Thu False 1 0.966 0.259 2 6 Thu False 1 1.000 0.000 3 9 Thu False 1 0.707 -0.707

Cyclical encoding with sine and cosine tells a model that 23:00 and 00:00 are neighbours — as plain numbers they'd look 23 apart.

Aggregations: From Events to One Row per Customer (RFM)

Cell — recency, frequency, monetary and morePython
feat = history.groupby("customer_id").agg(
    last_order=("order_time", "max"), first_order=("order_time", "min"),
    frequency=("amount", "size"), monetary=("amount", "sum"),
    avg_order=("amount", "mean"), max_order=("amount", "max"),
    discount_share=("discount", lambda d: (d > 0).mean()),
    electronics_share=("category", lambda c: (c == "Electronics").mean()))
feat["recency_days"] = (cutoff - feat.last_order).dt.days
feat["tenure_days"] = (cutoff - feat.first_order).dt.days
feat["orders_per_month"] = feat.frequency / (feat.tenure_days / 30).clip(lower=1)

last30 = history[history.order_time >= cutoff - pd.Timedelta(days=30)].groupby("customer_id").amount.sum()
prev30 = history[(history.order_time < cutoff - pd.Timedelta(days=30)) &
                 (history.order_time >= cutoff - pd.Timedelta(days=60))].groupby("customer_id").amount.sum()
feat["spend_trend"] = (last30.reindex(feat.index, fill_value=0) - prev30.reindex(feat.index, fill_value=0))
feat = feat.drop(columns=["last_order", "first_order"])
print(feat.round(2).head().to_string())
frequency monetary avg_order max_order discount_share electronics_share recency_days tenure_days orders_per_month spend_trend customer_id 1 7 5118.0 731.14 1592.0 0.86 0.14 10 144 1.46 1715.0 2 6 3036.0 506.00 1002.0 0.33 0.00 20 124 1.45 -30.0 4 14 6154.0 439.57 783.0 0.50 0.07 12 147 2.86 -747.0 5 5 2135.0 427.00 543.0 0.80 0.00 72 146 1.03 0.0 6 16 9553.0 597.06 1494.0 0.44 0.00 10 136 3.53 493.0

Ratios, Interactions and Flags

CellPython
feat["max_to_avg"] = (feat.max_order / feat.avg_order).round(2)            # one big order vs steady spending?
feat["value_x_recency"] = (feat.monetary / (1 + feat.recency_days)).round(1)
feat["rfm_segment"] = (pd.qcut(-feat.recency_days, 3, labels=["R1", "R2", "R3"]).astype(str) +
                       pd.qcut(feat.frequency.rank(method="first"), 3, labels=["F1", "F2", "F3"]).astype(str))
print(feat.rfm_segment.value_counts().head(5).to_dict())
print(feat[["recency_days", "frequency", "monetary", "max_to_avg", "rfm_segment"]].head(4).to_string())
{'R1F1': 60, 'R3F3': 56, 'R2F2': 38, 'R2F3': 31, 'R2F1': 30} recency_days frequency monetary max_to_avg rfm_segment customer_id 1 10 7 5118.0 2.18 R2F2 2 20 6 3036.0 1.98 R2F2 4 12 14 6154.0 1.78 R2F3 5 72 5 2135.0 1.27 R1F1

Label and Leakage

Cell — churn = no order in the 30 days after the cutoffPython
future = orders[(orders.order_time >= cutoff) & (orders.order_time < cutoff + pd.Timedelta(days=30))]
feat["churned"] = (~feat.index.isin(future.customer_id)).astype(int)
print(f"churn rate {feat.churned.mean():.1%}")
print(feat.groupby(pd.qcut(feat.recency_days, 4)).churned.mean().round(2).rename("churn rate by recency quartile").to_string())
churn rate 52.4% recency_days (-0.001, 6.0] 0.21 (6.0, 22.0] 0.40 (22.0, 61.0] 0.57 (61.0, 148.0] 0.94
Leakage = a feature that contains information you wouldn't have when making the real prediction. Here, any feature computed from orders after the cutoff (e.g. "total orders in June") would make the model look brilliant in testing and fail in production. Build features strictly from data before the prediction time.

Feature Ideas by Data Type

DataFeatures
Dates/timesHour, weekday, weekend, month, holiday/festival flag, days since/until, cyclical sin/cos
Transactions / eventsCounts, sums, means over windows (7/30/90 days), recency, trends, ratios
NumbersRatios (spend per visit), differences, log, bins, interactions
CategoriesEncodings, frequency, group statistics (average price in category)
TextLength, keyword flags, TF-IDF, embeddings (Module 9)
LocationDistance to store, city tier, cluster ID
Feature engineering derives informative inputs: date parts, weekend and holiday flags and cyclical sine/cosine encodings; aggregations that turn event logs into one row per entity, such as recency, frequency and monetary (RFM) values, windowed sums and trends; ratios, interactions and segment labels; and encodings and group statistics for categories. Features must be computed only from data available before the prediction time, with labels defined from a later window, to avoid leakage that inflates offline results and fails in production.
6.8

Matplotlib in Depth

Matplotlib is the foundation of Python plotting — Seaborn and pandas' .plot() are built on it. Module 1 covered single charts. Here you'll control layouts with several panels, annotate what matters, use twin axes and colour deliberately, and save publication-quality images. The key is the object-oriented interface: a Figure containing one or more Axes.

Anatomy

🖼️
Figure
The whole canvas: size, dpi, overall title, saving to file
📈
Axes (one per panel)
A plot area with its data, title, axis labels, ticks, legend and limits
✏️
Artists
Everything drawn: lines, bars, text, annotations, patches

A Multi-Panel Report Figure

Cell — subplot_mosaic, annotation, reference linesPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
months = pd.date_range("2025-07-01", periods=12, freq="MS")
revenue = np.array([42, 44, 47, 52, 61, 75, 58, 55, 60, 63, 66, 70]) * 1e5 * rng.uniform(0.97, 1.03, 12)
target = np.full(12, 55e5)
channels = pd.Series({"App": 46, "Website": 31, "Stores": 17, "Partners": 6})

fig, axd = plt.subplot_mosaic([["trend", "trend"], ["mix", "dist"]], figsize=(10, 6), constrained_layout=True)
ax = axd["trend"]
ax.plot(months, revenue, marker="o", color="#4ea8de", lw=2, label="revenue")
ax.plot(months, target, ls="--", color="#8da0b2", label="target ₹55 L")
ax.fill_between(months, revenue, target, where=revenue >= target, color="#6de5a0", alpha=0.2, interpolate=True)
peak = revenue.argmax()
ax.annotate("Diwali peak", xy=(months[peak], revenue[peak]), xytext=(months[peak - 3], revenue[peak] + 4e5),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#ffb454"), color="#ffb454")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"₹{v / 1e5:.0f} L"))
ax.set_title("Monthly revenue vs target", loc="left", fontweight="bold"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
for side in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)

ax = axd["mix"]
bars = ax.barh(channels.index, channels.values, color=["#4ea8de"] + ["#3a4a5a"] * 3)
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%d%%", padding=3); ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_title("Revenue share by channel", loc="left"); ax.set_xticks([])
for side in ("top", "right", "bottom"): ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)

ax = axd["dist"]
basket = rng.lognormal(6.5, 0.5, 3000)
ax.hist(basket, bins=40, color="#8e7cc3")
ax.axvline(np.median(basket), color="#ffb454"); ax.text(np.median(basket) * 1.05, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.85, f"median ₹{np.median(basket):.0f}", color="#ffb454")
ax.set_title("Basket value distribution", loc="left"); ax.set_xlabel("₹")
fig.suptitle("ShopSmart — FY26 snapshot", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")

Twin Axes and Saving

Cell — two units on one chart (use sparingly)Python
orders_k = revenue / 1e5 * 1.9 + rng.normal(0, 3, 12)
conv = np.array([2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.5, 2.9, 3.4, 2.6, 2.5, 2.7, 2.8, 2.9, 3.0])
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax1.bar(months, orders_k, width=20, color="#3a4a5a", label="orders (k)")
ax1.set_ylabel("orders (thousand)")
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(months, conv, color="#ffb454", marker="o", label="conversion %")
ax2.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(decimals=1)); ax2.set_ylabel("conversion")
fig.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.08, 0.95), frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("orders_conversion.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight")      # also .svg / .pdf for print
import os; print("saved:", os.path.getsize("orders_conversion.png") // 1024, "KB")
saved: 81 KB

Colour and Style Choices

  • Use one highlight colour for the point of the chart and greys for context (as in the channel bars above)
  • Sequential colormaps (viridis, Blues) for ordered values; diverging (coolwarm) for above/below a midpoint; qualitative (tab10) for categories
  • Prefer colour-blind-safe palettes and don't rely on red vs green alone
  • Remove chart junk: top/right spines, heavy gridlines, 3-D effects, redundant legends
  • Set a style once: plt.style.use(...) or plt.rcParams.update({...})
Matplotlib's object-oriented API organises a Figure containing Axes on which artists are drawn; subplots or subplot_mosaic with constrained_layout build multi-panel figures. Charts are made clearer with annotations and arrows, reference lines (axhline/axvline), fill_between for highlighted regions, bar_label for direct labels, tick formatters for currency and percentages, removed spines, and twin axes for two units used sparingly. Figures are exported with savefig at high dpi or as vector SVG/PDF, and colour choices should use sequential, diverging or qualitative colormaps that are colour-blind safe, with one highlight colour against grey context.
6.9

Seaborn

Seaborn sits on top of Matplotlib and speaks the language of DataFrames: pass a tidy (long) table and name the columns for x, y, colour (hue) and panels (col/row), and it handles grouping, colours, legends and statistical summaries like confidence bands. It's the fastest way to explore relationships between variables.

The Dataset

Cell — 800 restaurant ordersPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
sns.set_theme(style="darkgrid", rc={"axes.facecolor": "#161a22", "figure.facecolor": "#0e1015", "grid.color": "#2a2f3a",
                                    "text.color": "#e8eef5", "axes.labelcolor": "#e8eef5", "xtick.color": "#b5c7d6", "ytick.color": "#b5c7d6"})
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
n = 800
d = pd.DataFrame({"day": rng.choice(["Mon–Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"], n, p=[0.45, 0.17, 0.2, 0.18]),
                  "time": rng.choice(["Lunch", "Dinner"], n, p=[0.4, 0.6]),
                  "party": rng.choice([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], n, p=[0.1, 0.4, 0.15, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05])})
d["bill"] = (220 * d.party * np.where(d.time == "Dinner", 1.25, 1) * rng.lognormal(0, 0.25, n)).round()
d["tip"] = (d.bill * rng.normal(0.11, 0.03, n)).clip(0).round()
d["payment"] = rng.choice(["UPI", "Card", "Cash"], n, p=[0.55, 0.3, 0.15])
print(d.head(3).to_string())
day time party bill tip payment 0 Sun Lunch 4 1181.0 92.0 UPI 1 Mon–Thu Dinner 2 463.0 58.0 UPI 2 Fri Lunch 2 451.0 48.0 UPI

Distributions

Cell — histogram + KDE by group, box vs violinPython
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
sns.histplot(data=d, x="bill", hue="time", kde=True, element="step", ax=axes[0])
sns.boxplot(data=d, x="day", y="bill", hue="time", ax=axes[1], fliersize=2)
sns.violinplot(data=d, x="time", y="tip", inner="quartile", ax=axes[2], color="#4ea8de")
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["bill by time", "bill by day & time", "tip distribution"]): ax.set_title(t, fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()

Relationships

Cell — scatter with regression lines, split into panelsPython
g = sns.lmplot(data=d, x="bill", y="tip", hue="time", col="payment", height=3, aspect=1.1,
               scatter_kws={"s": 8, "alpha": 0.5})
g.set_titles("{col_name}")

One line of code produced three panels, colour by time, fitted regression lines and 95% confidence bands. That's Seaborn's main advantage: small multiples (col, row) for comparing groups side by side.

Categorical Summaries

Cell — means with confidence intervals; countsPython
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3))
sns.barplot(data=d, x="party", y="bill", hue="time", errorbar=("ci", 95), ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("average bill by party size (95% CI)", fontsize=10)
sns.countplot(data=d, x="day", hue="payment", ax=axes[1], order=["Mon–Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"])
axes[1].set_title("orders by day and payment", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()

Many Variables at Once

Cell — pair plot and an annotated heatmapPython
d["tip_pct"] = (d.tip / d.bill * 100).round(1)
g = sns.pairplot(d[["bill", "tip", "party", "tip_pct", "time"]], hue="time", corner=True, height=1.8,
                 plot_kws={"s": 6, "alpha": 0.5})

pivot = d.pivot_table(index="day", columns="party", values="bill", aggfunc="median").loc[["Mon–Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
sns.heatmap(pivot, annot=True, fmt=".0f", cmap="viridis", cbar=False, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("median bill (₹) by day and party size", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
QuestionSeaborn function
What does one variable look like?histplot, kdeplot, ecdfplot, displot
How does a number differ across groups?boxplot, violinplot, stripplot, barplot, pointplot
How do two numbers relate?scatterplot, regplot/lmplot, jointplot
Trend over time with uncertainty?lineplot (aggregates repeated x and adds a CI band)
Many variables?pairplot, heatmap, clustermap
Same chart per group?col=/row= on relplot, displot, catplot
Seaborn is a high-level statistical plotting library on Matplotlib that works directly with tidy DataFrames, mapping columns to x, y, hue, col and row. It provides distribution plots (histplot, kdeplot, box and violin plots), relationship plots (scatterplot, lmplot with regression lines and confidence bands, lineplot with aggregation), categorical summaries (barplot with confidence intervals, countplot), multi-variable views (pairplot, heatmap) and small multiples via figure-level functions; themes are set with set_theme, and the returned Matplotlib objects can be customised further.
6.10

Plotly: Interactive Charts

Static charts answer the question you designed them for. Plotly charts let the viewer ask their own: hover for exact values, zoom into a period, click legend items to hide series, and slide through time. They run in notebooks and browsers, export to standalone HTML, and power Dash web dashboards. The charts below are live — try hovering and zooming.

Plotly Express: One Line per Chart

Cell — daily orders by city with a range sliderPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio
pio.templates.default = "plotly_dark"

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
days = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", "2026-06-30", freq="D")
rows = []
for city, base in [("Hyderabad", 520), ("Bengaluru", 610), ("Chennai", 380)]:
    trend = np.linspace(0, 120, len(days))
    weekly = 60 * (days.dayofweek >= 5)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({"date": days, "city": city,
                              "orders": (base + trend + weekly + rng.normal(0, 35, len(days))).round()}))
daily = pd.concat(rows)
fig = px.line(daily, x="date", y="orders", color="city", title="Daily orders by city")
fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
fig.update_layout(height=380, margin=dict(l=40, r=20, t=50, b=20), hovermode="x unified")
fig.show()

Cell — product performancePython
products = pd.DataFrame({

monthly = (daily.assign(month=daily.date.dt.strftime("%Y-%m"))
                .groupby(["month", "city"], as_index=False).orders.sum())
fig = px.bar(monthly, x="city", y="orders", color="city", animation_frame="month",

Graph Objects for Full Control

Cell — combined bar + line with two y-axesPython
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
m = daily.groupby(daily.date.dt.to_period("M")).orders.sum()
conv = [2.4, 2.5, 2.7, 2.6, 2.9, 3.1]
fig = make_subplots(specs=[[{"secondary_y": True}]])
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=m.index.astype(str), y=m.values, name="orders", marker_color="#3a5a7a"), secondary_y=False)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=m.index.astype(str), y=conv, name="conversion %", mode="lines+markers",
                         line=dict(color="#ffb454", width=3)), secondary_y=True)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="orders", secondary_y=False); fig.update_yaxes(title_text="conversion %", secondary_y=True)
fig.update_layout(title="Orders and conversion", height=360, margin=dict(l=40, r=40, t=50, b=20))
fig.show()
fig.write_html("orders_conversion.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")      # share as a standalone file
print("saved interactive chart: orders_conversion.html")

Plotly produces interactive browser charts with hover tooltips, zoom, legend toggling, range sliders and animation. Plotly Express builds common charts from a DataFrame in one call (line, scatter with size and hover data, bar with animation_frame, treemap and sunburst for hierarchies), while graph_objects and make_subplots give full control such as secondary y-axes. Figures are customised with update_layout and update_xaxes, exported with write_html for standalone sharing, and form the basis of Dash and Streamlit dashboards; Matplotlib suits static publication figures and Seaborn fast statistical exploration.
6.11

Choosing the Right Chart & Visual EDA

Most bad charts are the wrong chart for the question. Start from what you want the viewer to see — a comparison, a trend, a distribution, a relationship, a composition — and the chart type follows. This lesson gives that mapping, the common traps, and a visual EDA routine that builds on the statistical EDA of Module 5 (lesson 5.14).

Question → Chart

You want to show…UseAvoid
Comparison across categoriesBar chart (horizontal for long labels), sorted; dot plot3-D bars, pie with many slices
Trend over timeLine chart; area for cumulative totalsBars for long daily series
DistributionHistogram, box/violin plot, ECDFBar of means only (hides spread)
Relationship between two numbersScatter (+ trend line); hexbin for many pointsTwo lines on twin axes implying correlation
Part of a wholeStacked bar, 100% bar, treemap; pie only for 2–4 partsDonut with 10 slices
RankingSorted horizontal bar, lollipopUnsorted bars
Two categorical dimensionsHeatmap, grouped barBig tables of numbers
GeographyChoropleth or point mapMaps when location isn't the point
Single numberKPI card with comparison (vs target/last period)Gauge charts

The Same Data, Better Chart

Cell — pie vs sorted barPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
share = pd.Series({"Grocery": 23, "Fashion": 21, "Electronics": 19, "Home": 15, "Beauty": 12, "Toys": 10})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
axes[0].pie(share, labels=share.index, startangle=90, textprops={"fontsize": 8})
axes[0].set_title("Which is bigger: Fashion or Electronics?", fontsize=10)
s = share.sort_values()
axes[1].barh(s.index, s.values, color=["#3a4a5a"] * 5 + ["#4ea8de"])
for i, v in enumerate(s.values): axes[1].text(v + 0.3, i, f"{v}%", va="center", fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_title("Sorted bars: differences are obvious", fontsize=10); axes[1].set_xticks([])
for side in ("top", "right", "bottom"): axes[1].spines[side].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()

Traps That Mislead

Cell — truncated axis and dual-axis illusionPython
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3))
vals = pd.Series({"Q1": 96.2, "Q2": 97.1, "Q3": 97.8})
axes[0].bar(vals.index, vals.values, color="#ff7c7c"); axes[0].set_ylim(96, 98)
axes[0].set_title("y starts at 96: looks like 8× growth", fontsize=9)
axes[1].bar(vals.index, vals.values, color="#6de5a0"); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 100)
axes[1].set_title("y starts at 0: +1.7% — honest", fontsize=9)

x = np.arange(12); a = 100 + 2 * x; b = 50 + 0.2 * x + np.random.default_rng(1).normal(0, 0.3, 12)
axes[2].plot(x, a, color="#4ea8de"); ax2 = axes[2].twinx(); ax2.plot(x, b, color="#ffb454")
axes[2].set_title("twin axes: any two rising lines 'match'", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
  • Bar charts must start at zero (bar length encodes the value); line charts may zoom in, but label clearly
  • Compare like with like: same scales across panels (sharey=True), per-capita or per-store rates rather than raw totals
  • Show uncertainty or spread, not just averages
  • Label units and time periods; put the source and date in a footnote

Visual EDA Routine

Cell — one function that profiles every column visuallyPython
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 1500
df = pd.DataFrame({"age": rng.integers(18, 70, n), "income_k": rng.lognormal(np.log(50), 0.5, n),
                   "city": rng.choice(["Hyderabad", "Bengaluru", "Chennai", "Pune"], n),
                   "visits": rng.poisson(6, n), "segment": rng.choice(["New", "Regular", "VIP"], n, p=[0.3, 0.6, 0.1])})
df["spend"] = 4 * df.income_k + 60 * df.visits + np.where(df.segment == "VIP", 600, 0) + rng.normal(0, 150, n)

def visual_profile(df, target):
    cols = [c for c in df.columns if c != target]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(cols), figsize=(3 * len(cols), 5.2))
    for i, c in enumerate(cols):
        top, bottom = axes[0, i], axes[1, i]
        if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[c]):
            top.hist(df[c], bins=30, color="#4ea8de")
            bottom.scatter(df[c], df[target], s=3, alpha=0.3, color="#4ea8de")
        else:
            counts = df[c].value_counts()
            top.bar(counts.index, counts.values, color="#8e7cc3")
            bottom.boxplot([df.loc[df[c] == k, target] for k in counts.index], tick_labels=counts.index, showfliers=False)
        top.set_title(c, fontsize=10); top.tick_params(labelsize=7); bottom.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    axes[1, 0].set_ylabel(target)
    plt.tight_layout()

visual_profile(df, "spend")

Top row: what each column looks like (skew in income, Poisson-shaped visits). Bottom row: how each relates to the target — income and visits clearly drive spend, VIPs spend more, while age and city show nothing. That's the shortlist of hypotheses to test formally (Module 5) or features to model (Module 7).

Chart choice follows the question: sorted bars for comparisons and rankings, lines for trends, histograms, box plots or ECDFs for distributions, scatter or hexbin for relationships, stacked or 100% bars and treemaps for composition (pies only for a few parts), heatmaps for two categorical dimensions and KPI cards for single numbers. Charts mislead through truncated bar axes, twin axes implying correlation, inconsistent scales, raw totals instead of rates, and averages without spread. A visual EDA routine plots each variable's distribution and its relationship to the target to generate hypotheses and candidate features.
6.12

Time Series Basics

A time series is a sequence of measurements in time order — daily sales, hourly website traffic, monthly churn. Order matters: today's value depends on yesterday's, and patterns repeat by week and year. This lesson covers pandas' time tools, the components of a series (trend, seasonality, noise), smoothing, lags and autocorrelation, and a first honest forecast.

Components

\[ y_t = \text{trend}_t + \text{seasonality}_t + \text{residual}_t \]additive model; when seasonal swings grow with the level, use multiplicative (or model log y)

Resampling and Rolling Windows

Cell — two years of daily salesPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
idx = pd.date_range("2024-07-01", "2026-06-30", freq="D")
t = np.arange(len(idx))
weekly = np.where(idx.dayofweek >= 5, 180, 0) + np.where(idx.dayofweek == 4, 60, 0)
yearly = 220 * np.exp(-((idx.dayofyear - 300) / 18.0) ** 2)                # festival season peak (Oct–Nov)
sales = pd.Series(1000 + 0.6 * t + weekly + yearly + rng.normal(0, 70, len(idx)), index=idx, name="sales").round()

print(sales.resample("ME").sum().tail(4).to_string())                     # month-end totals
print("\nby weekday (mean):", sales.groupby(sales.index.day_name().str[:3]).mean().round(0).to_dict())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
ax.plot(sales, lw=0.6, color="#3a5a7a", label="daily")
ax.plot(sales.rolling(7, center=True).mean(), color="#4ea8de", label="7-day mean")
ax.plot(sales.rolling(30, center=True).mean(), color="#ffb454", lw=2, label="30-day mean")
ax.legend(frameon=False); ax.set_title("Daily sales", loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()
2026-03-31 44190.0 2026-04-30 43545.0 2026-05-31 45743.0 2026-06-30 45022.0 Freq: ME by weekday (mean): {'Fri': 1300.0, 'Mon': 1238.0, 'Sat': 1416.0, 'Sun': 1419.0, 'Thu': 1244.0, 'Tue': 1236.0, 'Wed': 1246.0}

A 7-day window removes the weekly cycle; a 30-day window shows the trend and the festival peaks.

Decomposition

Cell — separate trend, weekly seasonality and residual (STL)Python
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
res = STL(sales, period=7, robust=True).fit()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(10, 6), sharex=True)
for ax, (name, s) in zip(axes, [("observed", sales), ("trend", res.trend), ("weekly", res.seasonal), ("residual", res.resid)]):
    ax.plot(s, lw=0.7, color="#4ea8de"); ax.set_ylabel(name, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
print("weekly effect by day:", res.seasonal.groupby(sales.index.day_name().str[:3]).mean().round(0).to_dict())
weekly effect by day: {'Fri': -2.0, 'Mon': -70.0, 'Sat': 124.0, 'Sun': 109.0, 'Thu': -56.0, 'Tue': -58.0, 'Wed': -46.0}

Lags, Differences and Autocorrelation

CellPython
frame = pd.DataFrame({"sales": sales, "lag_1": sales.shift(1), "lag_7": sales.shift(7),
                      "diff_1": sales.diff(1), "pct_vs_last_week": sales.pct_change(7, fill_method=None).round(3)})
print(frame.iloc[7:11].to_string())
print("\nautocorrelation:", {lag: round(float(sales.autocorr(lag)), 2) for lag in (1, 2, 6, 7, 14)})
sales lag_1 lag_7 diff_1 pct_vs_last_week 2024-07-08 912.0 1140.0 1000.0 -228.0 -0.088 2024-07-09 997.0 912.0 1074.0 85.0 -0.072 2024-07-10 1075.0 997.0 1053.0 78.0 0.021 2024-07-11 1004.0 1075.0 1052.0 -71.0 -0.046 autocorrelation: {1: 0.71, 2: 0.54, 6: 0.69, 7: 0.81, 14: 0.8}

Correlation with the value 7 days earlier is higher than with 6 days earlier — the weekly cycle. Lag features like these are what most forecasting models (and gradient-boosted trees) learn from.

A First Forecast — Evaluated Honestly

Cell — train on the past, test on the last 8 weeksPython
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
train, test = sales[:-56], sales[-56:]                      # never shuffle time series

forecasts = {
    "naive (yesterday)": pd.Series(train.iloc[-1], index=test.index),
    "seasonal naive (same weekday)": pd.Series(np.tile(train.iloc[-7:].to_numpy(), 8), index=test.index),
    "Holt-Winters": ExponentialSmoothing(train, trend="add", seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=7).fit().forecast(56),
}
for name, f in forecasts.items():
    mae = (f - test).abs().mean(); mape = ((f - test).abs() / test).mean()
    print(f"{name:<30} MAE {mae:6.1f}   MAPE {mape:.1%}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.8))
ax.plot(train[-90:], color="#8da0b2", label="history"); ax.plot(test, color="#e8eef5", label="actual")
ax.plot(forecasts["Holt-Winters"], color="#ffb454", label="Holt-Winters forecast")
ax.legend(frameon=False); plt.tight_layout()
naive (yesterday) MAE 91.6 MAPE 5.9% seasonal naive (same weekday) MAE 101.4 MAPE 6.9% Holt-Winters MAE 47.9 MAPE 3.2%
Always compare against a naive baseline. A model that can't beat "same as last week" isn't useful. And split by time — random splits leak the future into training.
pandas toolPurpose
pd.to_datetime, DatetimeIndex, .dtParse and access date parts
resample("W"/"ME"/"QE")Change frequency (aggregate)
asfreq, ffill, interpolateRegular spacing, fill gaps
rolling, ewmMoving averages, smoothing
shift, diff, pct_changeLags, changes, growth
tz_localize/tz_convertTime zones (store UTC, display IST)
A time series is ordered by time and typically combines trend, seasonality and residual noise, separated with decomposition such as STL (additive, or multiplicative when swings scale with level). pandas handles resampling to new frequencies, rolling and exponentially weighted means for smoothing, and shift, diff and pct_change for lags and growth; autocorrelation reveals cycles such as weekly patterns. Forecasts like Holt-Winters exponential smoothing must be evaluated on a time-based hold-out with MAE or MAPE against naive and seasonal-naive baselines, never with random splits.
6.13

Business KPIs

A metric is anything you can measure; a KPI (key performance indicator) is the handful of metrics tied directly to a business goal, with a target and an owner. Analysts spend much of their time defining KPIs precisely and computing them correctly — "active customer" or "revenue" can mean different things to different teams, and those differences change decisions.

Common KPIs by Area

AreaKPIDefinition
SalesRevenue / GMVSum of order value (state: before or after discounts, returns, tax)
Average order value (AOV)Revenue ÷ orders
Gross margin %(Revenue − cost of goods) ÷ revenue
MarketingConversion rateOrders (or buyers) ÷ visitors (sessions)
CACMarketing spend ÷ new customers acquired
CustomersRetention / churn rateShare of customers active in period t who are active (or not) in t + 1
Repeat purchase rateCustomers with 2+ orders ÷ all customers
Customer lifetime value (CLV)Expected margin from a customer over their lifetime
OperationsOn-time delivery %, return rateDelivered by promised time ÷ delivered; returned orders ÷ orders

Compute Them From Raw Data

Cell — orders and sessions for six monthsPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
n_cust = 4000
signup = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 181, n_cust), unit="D")
rows = []
for cid in range(n_cust):
    loyal = rng.random() < 0.35
    t = signup[cid]
    while t < pd.Timestamp("2026-07-01"):
        rows.append((cid, t))
        if rng.random() < (0.25 if loyal else 0.6):          # chance the customer never returns
            break
        t += pd.Timedelta(days=int(rng.exponential(25 if loyal else 45)) + 1)
orders = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["customer_id", "date"])
orders = orders[orders.date < "2026-07-01"].reset_index(drop=True)
orders["revenue"] = rng.lognormal(6.4, 0.5, len(orders)).round()
orders["cost"] = (orders.revenue * rng.uniform(0.62, 0.72, len(orders))).round()
orders["returned"] = rng.random(len(orders)) < 0.06
orders["month"] = orders.date.dt.to_period("M")
sessions = pd.Series(rng.integers(36_000, 44_000, 6), index=pd.period_range("2026-01", periods=6, freq="M"))
marketing = pd.Series([9.5, 9.0, 10.5, 11.0, 12.0, 12.5], index=sessions.index) * 1e5
print(len(orders), "orders from", orders.customer_id.nunique(), "customers")
7383 orders from 4000 customers
Cell — monthly KPI tablePython
kept = orders[~orders.returned]                                          # net of returns
first_month = orders.groupby("customer_id").month.min()
new_customers = first_month.value_counts().sort_index()

kpi = pd.DataFrame({
    "revenue_L": kept.groupby("month").revenue.sum() / 1e5,
    "orders": kept.groupby("month").size(),
    "buyers": kept.groupby("month").customer_id.nunique(),
    "margin_pct": 1 - kept.groupby("month").cost.sum() / kept.groupby("month").revenue.sum(),
    "return_rate": orders.groupby("month").returned.mean(),
    "new_customers": new_customers,
})
kpi["AOV"] = kpi.revenue_L * 1e5 / kpi.orders
kpi["conversion"] = kpi.orders / sessions
kpi["CAC"] = marketing / kpi.new_customers
kpi["revenue_MoM"] = kpi.revenue_L.pct_change()
fmt = {"revenue_L": "{:.1f}", "margin_pct": "{:.1%}", "return_rate": "{:.1%}", "AOV": "₹{:.0f}",
       "conversion": "{:.2%}", "CAC": "₹{:.0f}", "revenue_MoM": "{:+.1%}"}
print(kpi.apply(lambda col: col.map(lambda v: "—" if pd.isna(v) else fmt[col.name].format(v)) if col.name in fmt else col).to_string())

Retention: Cohort Analysis

A cohort is a group that started at the same time. A cohort table shows what share of each signup month is still buying 1, 2, 3… months later — the clearest view of whether the product keeps customers.

CellPython
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
o = orders.assign(cohort=orders.customer_id.map(first_month))
o["age_m"] = (o.month - o.cohort).apply(lambda x: x.n)
active = o.groupby(["cohort", "age_m"]).customer_id.nunique().unstack()
retention = active.div(active[0], axis=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.2))
sns.heatmap(retention, annot=True, fmt=".0%", cmap="Blues", cbar=False, ax=ax, annot_kws={"fontsize": 8})
ax.set_xlabel("months since first order"); ax.set_ylabel("cohort"); ax.set_title("Customer retention by cohort", loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()
print("average month-1 retention:", f"{retention[1].mean():.0%}")
average month-1 retention: 26%

Customer Lifetime Value (Simple Version)

\[ \text{CLV} \approx \frac{\text{AOV} \times \text{orders per month} \times \text{margin}\%}{\text{monthly churn rate}} \]expected monthly margin × expected lifetime in months (1 / churn) — a back-of-envelope figure to compare with CAC
CellPython
aov = kept.revenue.mean()
orders_per_active_month = (kept.groupby(["customer_id", "month"]).size()).mean()
margin = 1 - kept.cost.sum() / kept.revenue.sum()
churn = 1 - retention[1].mean()
clv = aov * orders_per_active_month * margin / churn
cac = (marketing.sum() / new_customers.sum())
print(f"AOV ₹{aov:.0f} · orders/active month {orders_per_active_month:.2f} · margin {margin:.1%} · monthly churn {churn:.0%}")
print(f"CLV ≈ ₹{clv:.0f}   CAC ≈ ₹{cac:.0f}   CLV/CAC = {clv / cac:.2f}  (healthy businesses aim for 3+)")
AOV ₹680 · orders/active month 1.24 · margin 32.9% · monthly churn 74% CLV ≈ ₹377 CAC ≈ ₹1612 CLV/CAC = 0.23 (healthy businesses aim for 3+)

The numbers tell a clear story: most customers buy once and leave, so each one is worth less than it costs to acquire. Improving month-1 retention is worth more than more marketing spend.

Defining a KPI Properly

FieldExample: "Monthly active customers"
Business questionIs our customer base growing?
Exact definitionDistinct customers with ≥ 1 non-returned order in the calendar month (IST)
Source and filtersorders table; excludes test accounts and staff orders
Target and owner+5% month on month; owned by the growth team
Guardrail metricMargin % — growth bought with deep discounts doesn't count
Pair every KPI with a guardrail. Optimise conversion alone and you may discount your margin away; optimise delivery speed alone and costs explode.
KPIs are the few metrics tied to business goals, each with an exact definition, data source and filters, target, owner and a guardrail metric. Common ones include revenue (stated net or gross of returns), average order value, gross margin, conversion rate, customer acquisition cost, retention and churn, repeat purchase rate, return rate and customer lifetime value. They are computed with grouped aggregations; cohort tables track the share of each starting cohort still active in later periods, and a simple CLV — AOV × purchase frequency × margin ÷ churn — compared with CAC shows whether acquisition is profitable.
6.14

Dashboards & Data Storytelling

A dashboard shows the current state of KPIs at a glance so people can monitor and act; a data story explains one insight and argues for one decision. Both fail the same way — too much on the page and no clear point. This lesson covers dashboard design, building one in Python, and turning an analysis into a story that gets acted on.

Dashboard vs Report vs Story

DashboardReportData story / presentation
PurposeMonitor KPIs, spot changesDocument results in detailDrive one decision
RefreshLive / dailyPeriodicOne-off
Audience action"Is anything off? Drill in."Read and reference"Approve / change X"

Dashboard Design Principles

1
Top row: KPI cards
4–6 headline numbers, each with a comparison (vs target, vs last period) and a colour only when action is needed
2
Middle: trends
How the main KPIs moved over time, with the target line
3
Bottom: breakdowns
By region, channel, product — where the change came from; filters for drill-down
  • Design for one audience and their decisions (CEO ≠ store manager)
  • Read top-left to bottom-right: most important first
  • Every number needs context: target, previous period, or benchmark
  • Consistent colours (one colour per category everywhere), few fonts, lots of white space
  • Show data freshness ("updated 18 Nov, 06:00 IST") and definitions on hover or in a glossary
