An Interactive Dashboard in Plotly

Cell — KPI indicators, trend and breakdown in one figurePython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
months = pd.period_range("2025-07", periods=12, freq="M").astype(str)
revenue = np.array([98, 101, 104, 112, 131, 148, 118, 115, 121, 126, 134, 142]) * 1e5 * rng.uniform(0.98, 1.02, 12)
target = np.array([100, 102, 105, 112, 128, 145, 120, 120, 125, 130, 138, 145]) * 1e5
regions = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["South", "West", "North", "East"], "growth": [0.09, 0.07, 0.04, -0.03]})

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=3, row_heights=[0.3, 0.7], column_widths=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3],
                    specs=[[{"type": "indicator"}, {"type": "indicator"}, {"type": "indicator"}],
                           [{"type": "xy", "colspan": 2}, None, {"type": "xy"}]],
                    subplot_titles=("", "", "", "Revenue vs target (₹)", "Revenue growth by region (MoM)"))
fig.add_trace(go.Indicator(mode="number+delta", value=revenue[-1] / 1e7, number={"prefix": "₹", "suffix": " Cr", "valueformat": ".2f"},
                           delta={"reference": revenue[-2] / 1e7, "relative": True, "valueformat": ".1%"}, title={"text": "Revenue (last month)"}), 1, 1)
fig.add_trace(go.Indicator(mode="number+delta", value=revenue[-1] / target[-1] * 100, number={"suffix": "%", "valueformat": ".0f"},
                           delta={"reference": 100}, title={"text": "% of target"}), 1, 2)
fig.add_trace(go.Indicator(mode="number+delta", value=7.4, number={"suffix": "%"},
                           delta={"reference": 6.0, "increasing": {"color": "#ff7c7c"}, "decreasing": {"color": "#6de5a0"}},
                           title={"text": "Return rate (limit 6%)"}), 1, 3)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=months, y=revenue, name="revenue", mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color="#4ea8de", width=3)), 2, 1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=months, y=target, name="target", line=dict(color="#8da0b2", dash="dash")), 2, 1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=regions.growth, y=regions.region, orientation="h", showlegend=False,
                     marker_color=["#6de5a0" if g > 0 else "#ff7c7c" for g in regions.growth],
                     text=[f"{g:+.0%}" for g in regions.growth], textposition="outside"), 2, 3)
fig.update_xaxes(tickformat=".0%", range=[-0.08, 0.14], row=2, col=3)
fig.update_layout(template="plotly_dark", height=520, title="ShopSmart — Monthly Business Review",
                  legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.08), margin=dict(l=40, r=30, t=70, b=40))
fig.show()

For filters and live data, the same figures go into a web app: Streamlit (simplest — a Python script becomes an app) or Dash (more control), or into BI tools (next lesson).

Data Storytelling: From Chart to Decision

Context
what the audience needs
→
Insight
one main finding
→
Evidence
the chart that proves it
→
Action
what to do, expected impact
Cell — the same data as an exploratory chart vs an explanatory chartPython
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
weeks = np.arange(1, 13)
rate = {"Bengaluru": 6.1 + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 12), "Chennai": 5.8 + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 12),
        "Pune": 6.0 + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 12),
        "Hyderabad": np.r_[6.0 + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 6), 9.5 + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 6)]}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4))
for city, r in rate.items():
    axes[0].plot(weeks, r, marker="o", label=city)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7); axes[0].grid(True); axes[0].set_title("Return rate by city (%)", fontsize=10)

ax = axes[1]
for city, r in rate.items():
    hl = city == "Hyderabad"
    ax.plot(weeks, r, color="#ff7c7c" if hl else "#4a5566", lw=3 if hl else 1.5)
    ax.text(12.3, r[-1], city, color="#ff7c7c" if hl else "#8da0b2", va="center", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold" if hl else "normal")
ax.axvline(6.5, color="#8da0b2", ls=":"); ax.text(6.6, 10.2, "new courier partner\nstarts (week 7)", color="#8da0b2", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Hyderabad returns jumped from 6% to 9.5% after the courier switch", loc="left", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(1, 14); ax.set_ylim(4.5, 11); ax.set_xlabel("week")
for side in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()

extra = (np.mean(rate["Hyderabad"][6:]) - 6.0) / 100 * 9_000 * 605       # weekly orders × AOV
print(f"cost of the extra returns ≈ ₹{extra:,.0f} per week")
cost of the extra returns ≈ ₹185,836 per week

The left chart is fine for finding the issue. The right one is built to tell it: the title states the conclusion, one colour highlights the story, direct labels replace the legend, and an annotation gives the cause. Add the cost and the recommendation ("review the courier contract; expected saving about ₹1.9 lakh a week") and you have a decision.

Storytelling Checklist

  • Lead with the answer (the "so what"), then the evidence — busy people may read only the first sentence
  • Chart titles that state the finding, not just the variables
  • One message per chart; highlight it, grey out the rest
  • Translate into the audience's units: rupees, customers, hours — not just percentages
  • Be honest about uncertainty and what the data can't tell you
  • End with a specific recommendation, owner and next step
Dashboards monitor KPIs for a specific audience, typically with a top row of KPI cards giving comparisons to target or prior period, trend charts in the middle and breakdowns with drill-down filters below, consistent colours and visible data freshness; in Python they can be built with Plotly indicators and subplots and served through Streamlit or Dash. Data storytelling moves from context to one insight, the evidence chart and a recommended action, using explanatory charts with conclusion titles, a single highlight colour, direct labels, annotations of causes and business impact in rupees, while acknowledging uncertainty.
6.15

Excel, Power BI & Tableau for Analysts

Python is the analyst's power tool, but most organisations consume analysis in Excel and BI platforms like Power BI and Tableau. Knowing how the same operations look in each — and how to hand data between them — makes your work usable by everyone. This lesson maps the concepts across tools and shows how to produce analyst-friendly Excel files from Python.

When to Use Which

ToolBest atLimits
ExcelQuick analysis, financial models, sharing small tables; everyone has it~1 million rows per sheet; manual steps hard to repeat and audit
Power BIInteractive dashboards on Microsoft data (Excel, SQL Server, Fabric); DAX measures; row-level securityDesktop app is Windows-only; DAX takes practice
TableauFast visual exploration and polished, highly interactive visualsLicence cost; complex calculations less natural than code
PythonAutomation, cleaning, statistics, ML, any data size (with the right engine)Needs coding; sharing requires apps or exports

The Same Operations in Each Tool

OperationpandasExcelPower BITableau
Load & cleanread_csv, .str, to_numericPower Query, TRIM, Text to ColumnsPower Query (M)Data Source, Tableau Prep
Lookup / joinmergeXLOOKUPRelationships in the modelRelationships / joins
Group & aggregategroupby().agg()PivotTable, SUMIFSMeasures: SUM, CALCULATEDrag dimension + measure
Conditional columnnp.whereIF, IFSCalculated column (DAX IF/SWITCH)Calculated field (IF … THEN)
Share of totaltransform("sum")=B2/SUM($B$2:$B$100)DIVIDE([Rev], CALCULATE([Rev], ALL(T)))Quick table calc: Percent of Total
Running total / YoYcumsum, pct_change(12)Formulas with relative rangesTime intelligence: TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEARTable calcs: Running Total, YoY
Group-level value on rowsgroupby().transform()SUMIFS per rowCALCULATE with ALLEXCEPTLOD: {FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Date])}

A Power BI Measure, Explained

Revenue = SUM ( Sales[Revenue] )

Revenue LY = CALCULATE ( [Revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )

Revenue YoY % = DIVIDE ( [Revenue] - [Revenue LY], [Revenue LY] )

Share of Region = DIVIDE ( [Revenue], CALCULATE ( [Revenue], ALL ( Stores[Region] ) ) )

Measures are calculated on the fly for whatever filters the visual applies (a month, a store, a slicer selection) — that "filter context" is the core idea of DAX. CALCULATE changes the filter context: ALL removes a filter to get the total; SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts dates. A proper model uses a star schema: a fact table (sales) linked to dimension tables (date, store, product, customer), plus a dedicated date table.

A Tableau Calculated Field and LOD Expression

// Calculated field: order size band
IF [Revenue] >= 5000 THEN "Large"
ELSEIF [Revenue] >= 1000 THEN "Medium"
ELSE "Small" END

// LOD: each customer's first purchase month (for cohort charts)
{ FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN(DATETRUNC('month', [Order Date])) }

From Python to an Analyst-Ready Excel Workbook

Cell — data sheet + summary with live formulas + formattingPython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from openpyxl import load_workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font, PatternFill
from openpyxl.formatting.rule import ColorScaleRule
from openpyxl.chart import BarChart, Reference

rng = np.random.default_rng(15)
data = pd.DataFrame({"Date": pd.date_range("2026-06-01", periods=60, freq="12h").date,
                     "Store": rng.choice(["Ameerpet", "Kukatpally", "Madhapur"], 60),
                     "Category": rng.choice(["Grocery", "Fashion", "Electronics"], 60),
                     "Revenue": rng.integers(800, 9000, 60)})
stores = sorted(data.Store.unique())

with pd.ExcelWriter("store_report.xlsx", engine="openpyxl") as xw:
    data.to_excel(xw, sheet_name="Data", index=False)
    pd.DataFrame({"Store": stores}).to_excel(xw, sheet_name="Summary", index=False)

wb = load_workbook("store_report.xlsx")
ws = wb["Summary"]
ws["B1"], ws["C1"] = "Revenue", "Share"
for r in range(2, len(stores) + 2):
    ws[f"B{r}"] = f"=SUMIFS(Data!$D:$D,Data!$B:$B,A{r})"            # live formula, not a pasted number
    ws[f"C{r}"] = f"=B{r}/SUM($B$2:$B${len(stores) + 1})"
    ws[f"B{r}"].number_format = "₹#,##0"; ws[f"C{r}"].number_format = "0.0%"
total_row = len(stores) + 2
ws[f"A{total_row}"], ws[f"B{total_row}"] = "Total", f"=SUM(B2:B{total_row - 1})"
ws[f"B{total_row}"].number_format = "₹#,##0"
for cell in ws[1] + ws[total_row]:
    cell.font = Font(bold=True)
for cell in ws[1]:
    cell.fill = PatternFill("solid", fgColor="DDEBF7")
ws.conditional_formatting.add(f"C2:C{total_row - 1}", ColorScaleRule(start_type="min", start_color="FFFFFF", end_type="max", end_color="63BE7B"))
ws.column_dimensions["A"].width = 14; ws.column_dimensions["B"].width = 14
wb["Data"].freeze_panes = "A2"; wb["Data"].auto_filter.ref = wb["Data"].dimensions

chart = BarChart(); chart.title = "Revenue by store"; chart.y_axis.title = "₹"
chart.add_data(Reference(ws, min_col=2, min_row=1, max_row=total_row - 1), titles_from_data=True)
chart.set_categories(Reference(ws, min_col=1, min_row=2, max_row=total_row - 1))
ws.add_chart(chart, "E2")
wb.save("store_report.xlsx")

check = load_workbook("store_report.xlsx")["Summary"]
for row in check.iter_rows(min_row=1, max_row=total_row):
    print(" | ".join(str(c.value) for c in row if c.value is not None))
print("pandas check of the same totals:", data.groupby("Store").Revenue.sum().to_dict(), "total", data.Revenue.sum())
Store | Revenue | Share Ameerpet | =SUMIFS(Data!$D:$D,Data!$B:$B,A2) | =B2/SUM($B$2:$B$4) Kukatpally | =SUMIFS(Data!$D:$D,Data!$B:$B,A3) | =B3/SUM($B$2:$B$4) Madhapur | =SUMIFS(Data!$D:$D,Data!$B:$B,A4) | =B4/SUM($B$2:$B$4) Total | =SUM(B2:B4) pandas check of the same totals: {'Ameerpet': 81122, 'Kukatpally': 72934, 'Madhapur': 128257} total 282313

The workbook keeps real Excel formulas, so colleagues can change the data and the summary updates — and they can see how every number was produced. The Data sheet has frozen headers and filters; the summary has formatting, a colour scale and a native chart.

Handing Data to BI Tools

  • Publish clean, modelled tables (a star schema) to a database, lakehouse or Parquet files — not one-off CSV exports
  • Put heavy cleaning in Python/SQL pipelines; keep BI for modelling measures and visuals
  • Use one shared date table and consistent keys across fact and dimension tables
  • Document KPI definitions once (semantic model) so every report computes them the same way
  • Power BI and Tableau can also run Python scripts and visuals — useful, but harder to maintain than upstream pipelines
Excel suits quick analysis and small shareable models (PivotTables, XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, Power Query); Power BI builds interactive dashboards on a star-schema model with DAX measures evaluated in filter context, where CALCULATE modifies filters for totals, shares and time intelligence; Tableau excels at visual exploration with calculated fields, table calculations and level-of-detail expressions such as FIXED. Python complements them for automation, cleaning, statistics and ML, can produce formatted Excel workbooks with live formulas and charts via openpyxl, and should feed BI tools with clean modelled tables and shared KPI definitions.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(616)

stores = pd.DataFrame({"store_code": ["HYD-01", "HYD-02", "HYD-03", "WGL-01", "KRM-01", "NZB-01"],
                       "store_name": ["Ameerpet", "Kukatpally", "LB Nagar", "Warangal", "Karimnagar", "Nizamabad"],
                       "city_tier": ["Metro", "Metro", "Metro", "Tier-2", "Tier-2", "Tier-2"]})
products = pd.DataFrame({
    "sku": [f"P{i:03d}" for i in range(1, 21)],
    "category": ["Staples"] * 6 + ["Dairy"] * 3 + ["Snacks"] * 4 + ["Personal care"] * 4 + ["Household"] * 3,
    "list_price": [420, 260, 180, 95, 310, 140, 62, 28, 240, 40, 20, 55, 99, 185, 120, 210, 85, 230, 160, 99],
    "unit_cost":  [370, 228, 156, 80, 268, 118, 54, 24, 205, 26, 13, 36, 66, 118, 75, 138, 52, 150, 104, 63]})

days = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", "2026-06-30", freq="D")
rows = []
for d in days:
    for s_i, store in enumerate(stores.store_code):
        n = rng.poisson(160 if s_i < 3 else 95)
        sku_idx = rng.choice(20, n, p=np.r_[[0.08] * 6, [0.07] * 3, [0.04] * 4, [0.03] * 4, [0.01] * 3])
        promo = (d.month >= 4) & (store in ("HYD-01", "HYD-02", "HYD-03")) & (sku_idx >= 9) & (sku_idx <= 16)
        disc = np.where(promo, 0.25, rng.choice([0, 0, 0, 0.05], n))
        qty = rng.integers(1, 4, n) + promo * rng.integers(0, 3, n)
        rows.append(pd.DataFrame({"bill_date": d.strftime("%d-%m-%Y"), "store": store,
                                  "sku": [f"P{i + 1:03d}" for i in sku_idx], "qty": qty, "discount_pct": disc}))
sales_raw = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
sales_raw.insert(0, "line_id", np.arange(1, len(sales_raw) + 1))                    # POS bill-line identifier
sales_raw.loc[rng.choice(len(sales_raw), 300, replace=False), "store"] = "hyd-02 "     # inconsistent codes
sales_raw.loc[rng.choice(len(sales_raw), 40, replace=False), "qty"] = 0                # voided lines
sales_raw = pd.concat([sales_raw, sales_raw.sample(500, random_state=1)], ignore_index=True)   # double-loaded batch
print(f"{len(sales_raw):,} sales lines · {len(stores)} stores · {len(products)} products")
print(sales_raw.head(3).to_string())
138,371 sales lines · 6 stores · 20 products line_id bill_date store sku qty discount_pct 0 1 01-01-2026 HYD-01 P006 1 0.00 1 2 01-01-2026 HYD-01 P004 1 0.05 2 3 01-01-2026 HYD-01 P008 3 0.00

2 · Clean and join

CellPython
before = len(sales_raw)
sales = (sales_raw
         .drop_duplicates()
         .assign(store=lambda d: d.store.str.strip().str.upper(),
                 bill_date=lambda d: pd.to_datetime(d.bill_date, format="%d-%m-%Y"))
         .query("qty > 0")
         .merge(products, on="sku", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
         .merge(stores, left_on="store", right_on="store_code", how="left", validate="many_to_one"))
assert sales.category.notna().all() and sales.store_name.notna().all(), "unmatched keys"

sales["revenue"] = sales.qty * sales.list_price * (1 - sales.discount_pct)
sales["cogs"] = sales.qty * sales.unit_cost
sales["gross_profit"] = sales.revenue - sales.cogs
sales["month"] = sales.bill_date.dt.to_period("M")
sales["quarter"] = "Q" + sales.bill_date.dt.quarter.astype(str)
print(f"{before:,} → {len(sales):,} rows (duplicates and voided lines removed); all keys matched")
print(sales[["bill_date", "store_name", "category", "qty", "discount_pct", "revenue", "gross_profit"]].head(3).round({"revenue": 1, "gross_profit": 1}).to_string())
138,371 → 137,831 rows (duplicates and voided lines removed); all keys matched bill_date store_name category qty discount_pct revenue gross_profit 0 2026-01-01 Ameerpet Staples 1 0.00 140.0 22.0 1 2026-01-01 Ameerpet Staples 1 0.05 90.2 10.2 2 2026-01-01 Ameerpet Dairy 3 0.00 84.0 12.0
Deduplication is safe here only because every row carries a unique POS line_id: two identical rows must be the same line loaded twice. Without such a key, two shoppers buying the same item on the same day would look like duplicates — ask the data owner before deleting anything that might be real.

3 · Headline KPIs: Q1 vs Q2

CellPython
def kpis(df):
    return pd.Series({"revenue_L": df.revenue.sum() / 1e5, "gross_profit_L": df.gross_profit.sum() / 1e5,
                      "margin_pct": df.gross_profit.sum() / df.revenue.sum(), "units_k": df.qty.sum() / 1e3,
                      "avg_discount": np.average(df.discount_pct, weights=df.qty * df.list_price)})
q = sales.groupby("quarter").apply(kpis, include_groups=False).T
q["change"] = q.Q2 / q.Q1 - 1
print(q.round(4).to_string())
quarter Q1 Q2 change revenue_L 226.2623 231.9606 0.0252 gross_profit_L 37.1734 33.3810 -0.1020 margin_pct 0.1643 0.1439 -0.1241 units_k 137.5010 150.6090 0.0953 avg_discount 0.0127 0.0466 2.6619

Confirmed: revenue up, gross profit down, margin down by about two percentage points. Now: where?

4 · Diagnose: which stores and categories?

Cell — margin by store tier × category, Q1 vs Q2Python
import seaborn as sns
seg = (sales.groupby(["quarter", "city_tier", "category"])
            .agg(revenue=("revenue", "sum"), gp=("gross_profit", "sum"))
            .assign(margin=lambda d: d.gp / d.revenue)
            .reset_index())
pivot = seg.pivot_table(index=["city_tier", "category"], columns="quarter", values="margin")
pivot["Δ pts"] = (pivot.Q2 - pivot.Q1) * 100
print((pivot.assign(Q1=pivot.Q1 * 100, Q2=pivot.Q2 * 100)).round(1).to_string())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
sns.heatmap(pivot["Δ pts"].unstack(), annot=True, fmt="+.1f", cmap="RdYlGn", center=0, cbar=False, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Change in gross margin, Q2 vs Q1 (percentage points)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlabel(""); ax.set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
quarter Q1 Q2 Δ pts city_tier category Metro Dairy 13.2 13.1 -0.0 Household 34.4 34.3 -0.1 Personal care 35.3 15.0 -20.4 Snacks 33.3 12.2 -21.2 Staples 12.0 12.1 0.0 Tier-2 Dairy 13.1 13.2 0.1 Household 34.3 34.4 0.0 Personal care 35.3 35.4 0.1 Snacks 33.3 33.3 0.0 Staples 12.0 12.1 0.0

The damage is concentrated: Snacks and Personal care in the Metro stores. Everything else is flat. What changed there in April?

Cell — discount depth and volume for the affected segment, by monthPython
affected = sales[(sales.city_tier == "Metro") & sales.category.isin(["Snacks", "Personal care"])]
m = affected.groupby("month").agg(units=("qty", "sum"), revenue=("revenue", "sum"), gp=("gross_profit", "sum"),
                                  promo_lines=("discount_pct", lambda d: (d >= 0.25).mean()))
m["margin"] = m.gp / m.revenue
print(m.assign(revenue=m.revenue.round(0), gp=m.gp.round(0)).round(3).to_string())

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
x = m.index.astype(str)
ax1.bar(x, m.units, color="#3a5a7a"); ax1.set_ylabel("units sold")
ax2 = ax1.twinx(); ax2.plot(x, m.margin * 100, color="#ff7c7c", marker="o", lw=2); ax2.set_ylabel("margin %")
pre, post = m.loc[:"2026-03"], m.loc["2026-04":]
ax1.set_title(f"Metro snacks & personal care: units {post.units.mean() / pre.units.mean() - 1:+.0%} from April, "
              f"margin {pre.margin.mean():.0%} → {post.margin.mean():.0%}", loc="left", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
units revenue gp promo_lines margin month 2026-01 8202 758360.0 262819.0 0.000 0.347 2026-02 7649 721154.0 249967.0 0.000 0.347 2026-03 8247 770001.0 267473.0 0.000 0.347 2026-04 11919 855866.0 120538.0 0.998 0.141 2026-05 12304 877068.0 123338.0 0.999 0.141 2026-06 12380 885022.0 124458.0 0.998 0.141

Did the promotion pay for itself?

Cell — compare with the same categories in Tier-2 stores (no promotion) as a controlPython
def q_gp(df): return df.groupby("quarter").gross_profit.sum()
metro = q_gp(affected)
control = q_gp(sales[(sales.city_tier == "Tier-2") & sales.category.isin(["Snacks", "Personal care"])])
expected_q2 = metro.Q1 * (control.Q2 / control.Q1)          # what Metro would have made following the control trend
impact = metro.Q2 - expected_q2
print(f"Metro Q1 gross profit ₹{metro.Q1:,.0f} → Q2 ₹{metro.Q2:,.0f}")
print(f"Tier-2 control trend: {control.Q2 / control.Q1 - 1:+.1%}  →  expected Metro Q2 ₹{expected_q2:,.0f}")
print(f"estimated promotion impact on gross profit: ₹{impact:,.0f} for the quarter")
total_drop = sales.groupby("quarter").gross_profit.sum().diff().iloc[-1]
print(f"total chain gross-profit change Q1→Q2: ₹{total_drop:,.0f}")
Metro Q1 gross profit ₹780,258 → Q2 ₹368,336 Tier-2 control trend: +0.9% → expected Metro Q2 ₹787,471 estimated promotion impact on gross profit: ₹-419,135 for the quarter total chain gross-profit change Q1→Q2: ₹-379,234

This is a difference-in-differences style estimate: the Tier-2 stores show what would have happened without the promotion. The 25% discount lifted volume, but not by nearly enough to cover the margin given away — the promotion explains essentially all of the chain's profit drop.

5 · The one-page dashboard

Cell — interactive summary for the regional headPython
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
monthly = sales.groupby("month").agg(revenue=("revenue", "sum"), gp=("gross_profit", "sum"))
monthly["margin"] = monthly.gp / monthly.revenue
cat_q = seg[seg.city_tier == "Metro"].pivot_table(index="category", columns="quarter", values="margin")

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=3, row_heights=[0.28, 0.72], column_widths=[0.34, 0.33, 0.33],
                    specs=[[{"type": "indicator"}] * 3, [{"type": "xy", "colspan": 2}, None, {"type": "xy"}]],
                    subplot_titles=("", "", "", "Monthly revenue (bars) and margin % (line)", "Metro margin by category"))
fig.add_trace(go.Indicator(mode="number+delta", value=q.loc["revenue_L", "Q2"], number={"prefix": "₹", "suffix": " L", "valueformat": ".1f"},
                           delta={"reference": q.loc["revenue_L", "Q1"], "relative": True, "valueformat": ".1%"}, title={"text": "Q2 revenue"}), 1, 1)
fig.add_trace(go.Indicator(mode="number+delta", value=q.loc["gross_profit_L", "Q2"], number={"prefix": "₹", "suffix": " L", "valueformat": ".1f"},
                           delta={"reference": q.loc["gross_profit_L", "Q1"], "relative": True, "valueformat": ".1%"}, title={"text": "Q2 gross profit"}), 1, 2)
fig.add_trace(go.Indicator(mode="number+delta", value=q.loc["margin_pct", "Q2"] * 100, number={"suffix": "%", "valueformat": ".1f"},
                           delta={"reference": q.loc["margin_pct", "Q1"] * 100, "valueformat": ".1f"}, title={"text": "Q2 margin"}), 1, 3)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=monthly.index.astype(str), y=monthly.revenue, name="revenue", marker_color="#3a5a7a"), 2, 1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=monthly.index.astype(str), y=monthly.margin * monthly.revenue.max() / 0.25, name="margin %",
                         mode="lines+markers+text", text=[f"{v:.1%}" for v in monthly.margin], textposition="top center",
                         line=dict(color="#ffb454", width=3)), 2, 1)
for qt, colour in [("Q1", "#8da0b2"), ("Q2", "#ff7c7c")]:
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(y=cat_q.index, x=cat_q[qt], name=f"margin {qt}", orientation="h", marker_color=colour), 2, 3)
fig.update_xaxes(tickformat=".0%", row=2, col=3)
fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=2.5, x1=2.5, y0=0, y1=1, xref="x", yref="y domain", line=dict(dash="dot", color="#8da0b2"))
fig.add_annotation(x=2.6, y=1.02, xref="x", yref="y domain", text="Metro 25% promo starts", showarrow=False, xanchor="left")
fig.update_layout(template="plotly_dark", height=560, barmode="group", title="DesiMart — Q2 margin review",
                  legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.08), margin=dict(l=40, r=30, t=70, b=40))
fig.show()

The story for the regional head

Cell — the summary, with every number computed from the dataPython
uplift = m.units.loc["2026-04":].mean() / m.units.loc[:"2026-03"].mean() - 1
print(f"""Q2 MARGIN REVIEW — DesiMart
The answer: Q2 revenue grew {q.loc['revenue_L', 'change']:+.1%} but gross profit fell {q.loc['gross_profit_L', 'change']:+.1%};
the April 25% promotion on snacks and personal care in the three Metro stores explains it.

Evidence
• Margin fell from {q.loc['margin_pct', 'Q1']:.1%} to {q.loc['margin_pct', 'Q2']:.1%}; the drop is concentrated in Metro snacks and personal care.
• Promotion lifted units in those categories by {uplift:.0%}, but at a 25% discount on ~{1 - products.iloc[9:17].unit_cost.sum() / products.iloc[9:17].list_price.sum():.0%} gross margin
  items, each extra sale earns far less than the discount gives away on sales we'd have made anyway.
• Against Tier-2 stores as a control, the promotion cost about ₹{-impact / 1e5:.1f} lakh of gross profit in the quarter.

Recommendation
1. End the blanket 25% discount; replace with a 10% loyalty-member offer and test it in one Metro store first (A/B by store).
2. Before any future promotion, require break-even volume: uplift needed = discount ÷ (margin − discount).
3. Add a weekly margin-by-category view to the store dashboard so this is caught in week 2, not quarter-end.""")
Q2 MARGIN REVIEW — DesiMart The answer: Q2 revenue grew +2.5% but gross profit fell -10.2%; the April 25% promotion on snacks and personal care in the three Metro stores explains it. Evidence • Margin fell from 16.4% to 14.4%; the drop is concentrated in Metro snacks and personal care. • Promotion lifted units in those categories by 52%, but at a 25% discount on ~36% gross margin items, each extra sale earns far less than the discount gives away on sales we'd have made anyway. • Against Tier-2 stores as a control, the promotion cost about ₹4.2 lakh of gross profit in the quarter. Recommendation 1. End the blanket 25% discount; replace with a 10% loyalty-member offer and test it in one Metro store first (A/B by store). 2. Before any future promotion, require break-even volume: uplift needed = discount ÷ (margin − discount). 3. Add a weekly margin-by-category view to the store dashboard so this is caught in week 2, not quarter-end.

Deliverables Checklist

  • Reproducible notebook or script: raw files in, clean tables and charts out
  • Data-quality log: duplicates, voided lines, inconsistent codes and what was done
  • KPI definitions used (revenue net of discount, gross profit = revenue − cost of goods)
  • One-page dashboard (Plotly HTML, or rebuilt in Power BI / Tableau from the clean tables)
  • Half-page written story: answer, evidence, recommendation, caveats

Extend It

  • Compute the break-even uplift per SKU and simulate discount levels from 5% to 30%
  • Add store-day weather or festival flags and re-check the promotion effect
  • Turn the dashboard into a Streamlit app with store and category filters
  • Export the clean fact and dimension tables to Parquet and build the same dashboard in Power BI
The DesiMart case study applies the full analysis workflow: loading raw POS extracts, cleaning inconsistent codes, voided lines and double-loaded duplicates, joining facts to product and store dimensions with key validation, engineering revenue, cost and gross-profit columns, comparing quarterly KPIs, localising a margin drop with segment heatmaps, explaining it with monthly volume and margin trends, estimating the promotion's impact against an untreated control group in a difference-in-differences style, and communicating through an interactive Plotly dashboard and a written story with a clear answer, evidence and recommendations.
